C.4 Proof of Proposition 3

Proof.

We construct a single-type instance in which the fluid equilibrium fits exactly in memory, but FCFS repeatedly selects the wrong finite batch composition. Let l=1l=1, l′=1l^{\prime}=1, and λ=4\lambda=4. Choose d1<1/24d_{1}<1/24 and set d0=1−12​d1d_{0}=1-12d_{1}. For this instance, the fluid equation is

n∗=λ⁡{d0+d1​(3​n∗)}.n^{*}=\lambda\{d_{0}+d_{1}(3n^{*})\}.

Thus n∗=4n^{*}=4, the equilibrium memory is M∗=3​n∗=12M^{*}=3n^{*}=12, and we set C=M∗=12C=M^{*}=12. The fluid batch composition is four prefill prompts and four decode prompts. It has selected memory 4+2⋅4=124+2\cdot 4=12, iteration time d0+12​d1=1d_{0}+12d_{1}=1, and completes Throughput∗=λ​l′=4\textbf{Throughput}^{*}=\lambda l^{\prime}=4 useful decode tokens per unit time.

First consider a decision epoch with no resident prompts and L≥12L\geq 12 prompts waiting externally for prefill. The integer LL is a fixed constant chosen below and does not depend on the time horizon TT. This state is feasible because external prefill-waiting prompts carry no resident KV cache. The selected batch composition space is finite: a batch can be represented by (b0,b1)(b_{0},b_{1}), the numbers of prefill and decode prompts selected, with feasibility condition

b0+2​b1≤12.b_{0}+2b_{1}\leq 12.

The unique full-throughput balanced composition is (4,4)(4,4). However, whenever FCFS reaches a decision epoch with no resident prompts and at least 12 external prompts waiting, it selects the batch (12,0)(12,0). This batch takes one unit of time and completes no prompt. After the prefill update, the 12 admitted prompts would occupy 2424 units of decode-stage KV cache, so the LIFO repair rule evicts six of them and leaves six decode-stage prompts resident. At the next decision epoch FCFS must batch those six resident decode prompts. Their selected memory is 1212, so no external prefill prompt can be admitted in the same iteration. This second batch also takes one unit of time and completes six prompts. The resident state is then empty again.

Thus, as long as the external queue has at least 12 prompts at the beginning of each empty-resident epoch, FCFS is trapped in the two-batch cycle

(12,0)⟶(0,6),(12,0)\quad\longrightarrow\quad(0,6),

which completes only six useful decode tokens in two units of time. Its throughput on this cycle is therefore 33, strictly below the fluid benchmark 44.

Starting from the empty system, this bad state is reached with a probability that is positive and independent of TT. Choose ε∈(0,d0+d1)\varepsilon\in(0,d_{0}+d_{1}), and let HLH_{L} be the event that at least L+12L+12 arrivals occur in [0,ε][0,\varepsilon]. Since LL is fixed, Pr⁡(HL)>0\Pr(H_{L})>0. On HLH_{L}, the first arrival starts a (1,0)(1,0) batch, and the other arrivals counted in HLH_{L} occur before that batch completes. Additional arrivals before the end of the warm-up can only increase the external queue. At the next decision epoch, FCFS has one decode prompt resident and at least L+11L+11 external prompts, so it selects (10,1)(10,1). After this batch, the old decode prompt completes and the ten admitted prompts would occupy 2020 units of decode-stage memory, so the repair rule evicts four and leaves six decode prompts resident. The next batch is therefore (0,6)(0,6), because these six decode prompts already use all 1212 units of selected memory. Let σ\sigma be the decision epoch after this third batch. Then σ≤ε+3\sigma\leq\varepsilon+3, the resident state is empty, and the external queue has at least LL prompts. The seven completions during this warm-up are a bounded end effect.

It remains to show that, once reached, this cycle has positive probability of persisting over the whole horizon. Let QrQ_{r} be the external queue length at the beginning of the rr-th empty-resident epoch after time σ\sigma, under the saturated evolution described above. If Qr≥12Q_{r}\geq 12, then over the next two one-unit iterations the system consumes 12 external prompts, returns six evicted prompts to the external queue, and receives Ar∼Poisson⁡(8)A_{r}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(8) new external arrivals. By the strong Markov property and independent increments of the Poisson arrival process, the variables ArA_{r} are iid after σ\sigma. Hence

Qr+1=Qr−6+Ar.Q_{r+1}=Q_{r}-6+A_{r}.

The increments Ar−6A_{r}-6 have positive mean 22 and finite exponential moments. A random walk with such increments has a strictly positive probability of never crossing any fixed lower level when it is started sufficiently far above that level; moreover this survival probability tends to one as the initial offset grows. Therefore, for a sufficiently large fixed LL,

pL:=Pr{L+∑u=0r−1(Au−6)≥12 for all r≥0}>0p_{L}:=\Pr\left\{L+\sum_{u=0}^{r-1}(A_{u}-6)\geq 12\text{ for all }r\geq 0\right\}>0

by the standard positive-survival property of a random walk with positive drift. Fix such an LL for the rest of the proof.

Let ELE_{L} be the event that HLH_{L} occurs and that this post-σ\sigma random walk never falls below 12. Since on HLH_{L} we have Q0≥LQ_{0}\geq L, monotonicity of the recursion gives a conditional survival probability at least pLp_{L}, and hence

Pr⁡(EL)≥Pr⁡(HL)​pL>0.\Pr(E_{L})\geq\Pr(H_{L})p_{L}>0.

On ELE_{L}, after the bounded warm-up time σ\sigma, FCFS remains in the two-batch cycle forever and completes six one-token prompts every two units of time. Thus C⁡(T)/T→3C(T)/T\to 3 on ELE_{L}; the bounded warm-up completions and any incomplete terminal cycle contribute only O⁡(1/T)O(1/T). Also, by the strong law of large numbers for the Poisson arrivals, A⁡(T)/T→4A(T)/T\to 4 almost surely. Hence, on ELE_{L} up to a null set,

limT→∞A⁡(T)−C⁡(T)T=4−3=1.\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{A(T)-C(T)}{T}=4-3=1.

Let XT=(A⁡(T)−C⁡(T))/TX_{T}=(A(T)-C(T))/T. Since the system starts empty and each completed prompt must have arrived exogenously, C⁡(T)≤A⁡(T)C(T)\leq A(T) pathwise, so XT≥0X_{T}\geq 0. Moreover, all outputs have length one, Throughput∗=𝔼⁡[A⁡(T)]/T=4\textbf{Throughput}^{*}=\mathbb{E}[A(T)]/T=4, and 𝔼⁡[Throughput(T,FCFS)]=𝔼⁡[C⁡(T)]/T\mathbb{E}[\textbf{Throughput}^{(T,\mathrm{FCFS})}]=\mathbb{E}[C(T)]/T. Therefore Fatou’s lemma gives

lim infT→∞{Throughput∗−𝔼⁡[Throughput(T,FCFS)]}\displaystyle\liminf_{T\to\infty}\left\{\textbf{Throughput}^{*}-\mathbb{E}[\textbf{Throughput}^{(T,\mathrm{FCFS})}]\right\} =lim infT→∞𝔼⁡[XT]\displaystyle=\liminf_{T\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[X_{T}]
≥lim infT→∞𝔼⁡[XT​𝟏EL]\displaystyle\geq\liminf_{T\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[X_{T}\mathbf{1}_{E_{L}}]
≥𝔼⁡[lim infT→∞XT​𝟏EL]=Pr⁡(EL)>0.\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}\left[\liminf_{T\to\infty}X_{T}\mathbf{1}_{E_{L}}\right]=\Pr(E_{L})>0.

This gives

Throughput∗−𝔼⁡[Throughput(T,FCFS)]=Ω⁡(1),\textbf{Throughput}^{*}-\mathbb{E}[\textbf{Throughput}^{(T,\mathrm{FCFS})}]=\Omega(1),

as claimed. ∎

C.5 Proof of Proposition 6

Proof.

We construct a two-output-length instance in which the known-type fluid equilibrium fits exactly in memory, but every non-predictive rule loses a constant amount of useful service in each saturated boundary block. Repeating these blocks gives the long-run gap, as in the proof of Proposition 3.

Consider two prompt types with the same observable input features, the same prefill length, and the same first decode token. Type 1 completes after the first decode token, whereas type 2 continues to one additional decode stage. There is no side information correlated with the hidden type. Let a newly admitted prompt be type 2 with probability p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), independently across prompts, and suppose the type is not revealed until the prompt either completes at the first boundary or survives into the second segment. Choose the arrival rates and service parameters so that the known-type fluid equilibrium is integral over one comparison block of length Δ\Delta: the block receives mean BB new prompts, advances BB unrevealed prompts across the first boundary, and allocates downstream capacity for s=p​Bs=pB long survivors, where BB and ss are integers. We choose the fixed parameters generically so that, among feasible finite selected-composition sequences in this block, this known-type composition is the unique sequence attaining the fluid useful-service count. Set the physical memory to the corresponding known-type requirement C=M∗C=M^{*}. At this boundary value the fluid block also contains a deterministic resident composition from the other prefill/decode stages, and this composition together with the BB boundary crossings and ss downstream slots exactly exhausts the memory budget.

We first prove a one-block lower bound. Consider a comparison block that begins with the deterministic resident composition and at least BB unrevealed prompts available at the first-segment entry. Within a block of length Δ\Delta, any feasible policy can execute only finitely many nonempty iterations, because each nonempty iteration takes at least d0>0d_{0}>0, and each selected batch has finitely many integer compositions because C<∞C<\infty and every resident prompt has positive memory. Thus the possible selected-composition sequences in the block form a finite set. Any sequence that differs from the known-type fluid composition by omitting, delaying, or evicting part of the deterministic resident work, or by advancing fewer than BB unrevealed prompts across the first boundary, completes at least one fewer useful decode token than the fluid block. Since the action set is finite, all such off-fluid sequences have a uniform positive useful-service deficit.

It remains only to analyze the unique no-immediate-loss candidate: the policy advances exactly BB unrevealed prompts across the first boundary while reserving downstream room for exactly ss long survivors. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be the sigma-field generated by the policy’s observations just before this boundary revelation, including past arrivals, past boundary revelations, the current queues, and any internal randomization already realized by the policy. Conditional on ℱ\mathcal{F}, non-predictiveness implies that the number of selected prompts that survive the boundary is

YB∼Binomial⁡(B,p),Y_{B}\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(B,p),

independently of ℱ\mathcal{F}. Since s=p​Bs=pB and 0<p<10<p<1, YBY_{B} has nonzero variance and

ρ:=Pr{YB>s}>0.\rho:=\Pr\{Y_{B}>s\}>0.

On this event the realized survivor count exceeds the downstream capacity present at C=M∗C=M^{*}. Therefore at least one survivor must be evicted and restarted, or retained as unfinished downstream work that displaces useful service from the current fluid block. Thus the saturated block has a positive lower bound on the expected sum of current useful-service deficit and displaced-work carryover.

It remains to make this block argument repeatable under arbitrary policy-induced states. We use a finite augmented block MDP. The augmentation only helps the controller: at the beginning of each comparison block it may see all arrivals that occur during that block and may use them immediately, but it still does not observe an unrevealed prompt’s output length before the first boundary. A lower bound for this augmented controller is therefore a lower bound for the original online policies.

Let NΔ=⌊Δ/d0⌋+1N_{\Delta}=\lfloor\Delta/d_{0}\rfloor+1. In one block there are at most NΔN_{\Delta} nonempty iteration starts, up to one residual iteration may cross a block boundary, and each feasible resident list has bounded length because every resident prompt has positive KV-cache size and total memory is at most CC. Choose finite caps HH and HAH_{A} larger than the maximum number of prompt-stage advances, evictions, external arrivals, or deferred first-segment-equivalent units that can affect one block. Work or arrivals beyond these caps can only help fill the saturated first-segment pool or increase future displaced work, so truncating them at the cap cannot make the lower bound harder. At the beginning of block rr, define the capped state

Sr=(Rr,Qr,Er,Ur),S_{r}=(R_{r},Q_{r},E_{r},U_{r}),

where RrR_{r} is the resident list, including each prompt’s revealed segment/stage and any eviction priority relevant to the policy, QrQ_{r} is the capped number of unrevealed prompts available at the first-segment entry, ErE_{r} is the capped amount of restarted or deferred work that can displace work in later blocks, and UrU_{r} records the finite residual in-service composition and remaining service category from an iteration crossing the block boundary. This state space is finite. The saturated fluid state s⋆s^{\star} has the deterministic fluid resident composition, Q=BQ=B, E=0E=0, and no residual cross-boundary service.

For each capped state xx, a pure block action is a nonanticipative decision tree that, for at most NΔN_{\Delta} within-block decision epochs, maps the finite capped within-block observation history to feasible admission, batching, preemption, and eviction decisions. The action may use all capped arrivals in the block from time zero, by the augmentation, but it cannot use unrevealed output-length labels before boundary revelation. Hence each 𝒜¯​(x)\bar{\mathcal{A}}(x) is finite. Dependence on prompt identities, arrival times, older history, or internal randomization does not enlarge this finite model: conditional on the full observable history, any non-predictive selection of unrevealed prompts has conditionally i.i.d. Bernoulli-pp continuation indicators, and only the capped selected composition and revealed boundary outcomes affect the transition kernel and useful-service count. Let GrG_{r} be the useful-service deficit in block rr relative to the known-type fluid block, with tokens from evicted prompts counted as useless as in Section 2.

We next rule out zero-average recurrent classes in this finite augmented model. By the generic choice of parameters, from s⋆s^{\star} the only way to have zero one-block deficit before the boundary revelation is to execute the unique fluid selected-composition sequence: serve all deterministic resident work, advance exactly BB unrevealed prompts across the first boundary, and reserve exactly s=p​Bs=pB downstream survivor slots. From any other capped state, or under any other pure block action, either the block immediately misses at least one unit of useful service, or it spends service repairing a resident-composition, backlog, residual-service, or displaced-work mismatch. Except for the displaced-work buffer discussed next, any zero-current-deficit repair transition must strictly decrease the finite rank

R⁡(x):=resident-composition shortfall+(B−Q)++residual-service mismatch.R(x):=\text{resident-composition shortfall}+(B-Q)^{+}+\text{residual-service mismatch}.

Thus any closed zero-average class must reduce to the saturated resident/backlog/residual configuration, with only the displaced-work buffer E∈{0,…,H}E\in\{0,\ldots,H\} possibly varying, and must use the fluid selected-composition sequence whenever it seeks zero current deficit.

On this reduced class, conditional on the full block-start history and on any realized internal randomization before the boundary decision, non-predictiveness gives YB∼Binomial⁡(B,p)Y_{B}\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(B,p) for the BB boundary-crossing prompts. Let Z=YB−sZ=Y_{B}-s. Then 𝔼⁡[Z]=0\mathbb{E}[Z]=0, and because 0<p<10<p<1 and s=p​B∈{1,…,B−1}s=pB\in\{1,\ldots,B-1\}, Pr{Z>0}>0\Pr\{Z>0\}>0 and Pr{Z<0}>0\Pr\{Z<0\}>0. If the block has displaced-work level EE, the best zero-deficit use of old displaced work can only update the buffer as a finite reflected queue,

E+=min⁡{H,max⁡{0,E+Z}},E^{+}=\min\{H,\max\{0,E+Z\}\},

with boundary loss at least

L⁡(E,Z)=(E+Z−H)++(−E−Z)+.L(E,Z)=(E+Z-H)^{+}+(-E-Z)^{+}.

The upper-boundary term is excess long-survivor work that cannot fit in memory at C=M∗C=M^{*} even after using the finite buffer; it must be evicted, restarted, or pushed beyond the capped recoverable workload, losing useful service. The lower-boundary term is an unused downstream survivor slot when current survivors plus displaced work are insufficient, leaving part of the fluid block’s useful service unfilled. Since the finite reflected chain driven by ZZ has both upward and downward moves with positive probability, every closed recurrent class has positive stationary probability of a boundary loss. Hence the average of L⁡(E,Z)L(E,Z), and therefore the average one-block useful-service deficit, is strictly positive on this reduced class. Combining this with the rank argument for all other states shows that every recurrent class of every stationary deterministic selector has strictly positive average one-block deficit. Since the finite augmented MDP has finitely many stationary deterministic selectors and recurrent classes, the minimum average deficit is some ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

By the finite-state average-cost optimality equations, equivalently the dual of the average-cost linear program, there exists a bounded potential Φ\Phi on capped states such that, for every capped state xx and every pure block action a∈𝒜¯​(x)a\in\bar{\mathcal{A}}(x),

𝔼[Gr+Φ(Sr+1)−Φ(Sr)∣Sr=x,a]≥ϵ.\mathbb{E}\!\left[G_{r}+\Phi(S_{r+1})-\Phi(S_{r})\mid S_{r}=x,\ a\right]\geq\epsilon.

Now fix any randomized history-dependent non-predictive policy. Conditional on the full block-start history ℱr\mathcal{F}_{r}, the policy induces a probability distribution over the finite set of pure block actions available at SrS_{r}. Averaging the preceding inequality over this distribution gives

𝔼⁡[Gr+Φ⁡(Sr+1)−Φ⁡(Sr)∣ℱr]≥ϵ\mathbb{E}\!\left[G_{r}+\Phi(S_{r+1})-\Phi(S_{r})\mid\mathcal{F}_{r}\right]\geq\epsilon

in every block.

Summing the displayed inequality over the RT=T/Δ+O⁡(1)R_{T}=T/\Delta+O(1) complete comparison blocks and using boundedness of Φ\Phi gives

𝔼⁡[∑r=0RT−1Gr]≥ϵ​RT−O⁡(1).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{r=0}^{R_{T}-1}G_{r}\right]\geq\epsilon R_{T}-O(1).

Hence the accumulated effective-throughput deficit is Ω⁡(T)\Omega(T). On every sample path, the completed-token rate is bounded by a finite constant RmaxR_{\max} because each nonempty iteration completes at most CC one-token decode steps and takes at least d0d_{0} time. As in Proposition 3, bounded end effects therefore give

Throughput∗−𝔼⁡[Throughput(T,π)]≥ϵ0−O⁡(1/T)=Ω⁡(1)\textbf{Throughput}^{*}-\mathbb{E}[\textbf{Throughput}^{(T,\pi)}]\geq\epsilon_{0}-O(1/T)=\Omega(1)

for some ϵ0>0\epsilon_{0}>0 depending only on the constructed instance. ∎

Appendix D Proof of Theorem 4

This proof establishes the WAIT performance bounds when output lengths are known. The argument proceeds in two parts:

  1. 1.

    Single-type case: We construct a coupled dominating process using the Lindley recursion and apply Kingman’s bound for queue length expectations.

  2. 2.

    Multiple-type case: We construct an auxiliary embedded full-threshold process and couple it to event-driven WAIT type by type. This embedded process separates stochastic entry accumulation from the event-driven batch composition while preserving the service opportunities created by the WAIT thresholds.

Key techniques include: Lindley recursion for queue length bounds (Asmussen, 2003, Proposition 6.3), coupling construction to dominate the original process, Kingman’s bound for negative drift processes (Kingman, 1962), and standard random walk results (Strait, 1974).

Throughout this appendix, we use bb to denote the index of the embedded full-threshold review epochs, which is distinct from the stage index s∈{0,1,…,lj′}s\in\{0,1,\ldots,l_{j}^{\prime}\} used in the main text for decode stages. We use tt for continuous time and BB for the number of embedded review intervals.

We first consider the single-type case, then extend to multiple types.

D.0.1 Single-Type Case

Consider a single prompt type with threshold nn. For general scheduling algorithms, analyzing this system in continuous time is challenging: KV cache grows dynamically during decode, arrivals are stochastic, and eviction risks complicate the dynamics.

The WAIT policy’s threshold mechanism achieves a dimensionality reduction. By waiting until exactly nn prompts accumulate before initiating a batch, the algorithm enforces a fixed batch size, which ensures constant processing time Δ​T\Delta T per batch. This decouples the continuous-time memory-constrained dynamics into a tractable discrete-time process: a memory-constrained queueing system becomes a simple random walk. The reduction is enabled by the algorithm design and is what makes the subsequent drift analysis apply.

Specifically, let λ~\tilde{\lambda} denote the continuous-time arrival rate and let μ=λ~​Δ​T\mu=\tilde{\lambda}\Delta T be the expected number of arrivals during a threshold-sized batch. The boundary case is μ=n\mu=n. For this preliminary calculation, view time through deterministic full-threshold review intervals of length Δ​T\Delta T, rather than through the exact event-driven batch-completion clock. The embedded review process, indexed by b∈ℕb\in\mathbb{N}, is a zero-drift threshold queue. A review slot is “stuck” if fewer than nn prompts are available at that review. This is the single-type version of the embedded comparison process used in the formal multi-type proof below.

Lemma 10 (Queue Length and Stuck Time).

This lemma connects queue accumulation to stuck review slots in the critical case μ=n\mu=n. Let XbX^{b} denote the number of arrivals during review interval bb, where Xb∼Poisson⁡(n)X^{b}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(n). Let WbW^{b} denote the residual queue length after review bb, with W0=0W^{0}=0. The state transition is:

Wb+1=Wb+Xb−n⋅𝟏{Wb+Xb≥n}.W^{b+1}=W^{b}+X^{b}-n\cdot\mathbf{1}\{W^{b}+X^{b}\geq n\}.

Define B​s​t​u​c​kB_{\emph{stuck}} as the number of stuck review slots, where Wb+Xb<nW^{b}+X^{b}<n. Then:

𝔼⁡[WB]=n⋅𝔼⁡[B​s​t​u​c​k].\mathbb{E}[W^{B}]=n\cdot\mathbb{E}[B_{\emph{stuck}}].

The proof is in Appendix G.1. This lemma connects queue accumulation to missed threshold removals in the embedded review process. To bound 𝔼⁡[WB]\mathbb{E}[W^{B}], we construct a coupled dominating process that admits tractable analysis via classical queueing techniques.

Lemma 11 (Coupled Dominating Process).

The coupled process starts with a safety buffer (2​n2n versus 0) and maintains dominance throughout. Define {W~b}\{\tilde{W}^{b}\} by:

W~0=2​n,W~b+1=max⁡{2​n,W~b+Xb−n}.\tilde{W}^{0}=2n,\quad\tilde{W}^{b+1}=\max\{2n,\tilde{W}^{b}+X^{b}-n\}.

Then W~b≥Wb+n\tilde{W}^{b}\geq W^{b}+n for all b∈ℕb\in\mathbb{N}.

The proof is in Appendix G.2.

Lindley recursion.

To analyze the coupled process, we apply the Lindley recursion representation (Asmussen, 2003, Proposition 6.3):

Lemma 12 (Lindley Representation).

Let Sk=∑r=1k(Xr−n)S^{k}=\sum_{r=1}^{k}(X^{r}-n) be the partial sum process. Then:

W~B=2​n+max⁡(SB,SB−S1,…,SB−SB−1,0).\tilde{W}^{B}=2n+\max(S^{B},S^{B}-S^{1},\ldots,S^{B}-S^{B-1},0).

This classical queueing representation is made applicable by the WAIT policy’s threshold design. Define ξk=Xk−n\xi^{k}=X^{k}-n. We use time-reversal symmetry to simplify the maximum expression:

max⁡(SB,SB−S1,…,SB−SB−1,0)=max1≤k≤B⁡(∑r=kBξr)+​=𝑑​max1≤k≤B​(∑r=1kηr)+,ηr​=𝑑​X1−n.\max(S^{B},S^{B}-S^{1},\ldots,S^{B}-S^{B-1},0)=\max_{1\leq k\leq B}\Big(\sum_{r=k}^{B}\xi^{r}\Big)^{+}\overset{d}{=}\max_{1\leq k\leq B}\Big(\sum_{r=1}^{k}\eta^{r}\Big)^{+},\quad\eta^{r}\overset{d}{=}X^{1}-n.

Thus W~B​=𝑑​2​n+max1≤k≤B⁡(∑r=1kηr)+\tilde{W}^{B}\overset{d}{=}2n+\max_{1\leq k\leq B}(\sum_{r=1}^{k}\eta^{r})^{+}.

Since W~B≥WB+n\tilde{W}^{B}\geq W^{B}+n, we have 𝔼⁡[WB]≤𝔼⁡[W~B]−n\mathbb{E}[W^{B}]\leq\mathbb{E}[\tilde{W}^{B}]-n. Let YB=max1≤k≤B⁡(∑r=1kηr)+Y^{B}=\max_{1\leq k\leq B}(\sum_{r=1}^{k}\eta^{r})^{+}. By (Strait, 1974, Lemma 2):

Lemma 13 (Random Walk Maximum).
𝔼⁡[YB]=𝔼⁡[max1≤k≤B⁡(Sk)+]=∑k=1B1k​𝔼​[(Sk)+].\mathbb{E}\left[Y^{B}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{1\leq k\leq B}(S^{k})^{+}\right]=\sum_{k=1}^{B}\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{E}\left[(S^{k})^{+}\right].

This standard result (Strait, 1974) decomposes the maximum into a sum over batch indices. For 𝔼⁡[(Sk)+]\mathbb{E}[(S^{k})^{+}], the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and Var⁡(Sk)=n​k\mathrm{Var}(S^{k})=nk imply 𝔼⁡[(Sk)+]≤n​k\mathbb{E}[(S^{k})^{+}]\leq\sqrt{nk}. Hence:

𝔼[YB]≤n∑k=1Bk−1/2=O(n​B).\mathbb{E}[Y^{B}]\leq\sqrt{n}\sum_{k=1}^{B}k^{-1/2}=O(\sqrt{nB}).
Lemma 14 (Throughput Gap Bound).
𝔼⁡[WB]−n≤𝔼⁡[YB]≤n​∑k=1B1k=O⁡(n​B).\mathbb{E}[W^{B}]-n\leq\mathbb{E}[Y^{B}]\leq\sqrt{n}\sum_{k=1}^{B}\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}=O(\sqrt{nB}).

By Lemma 10, the expected number of stuck review slots is 𝔼⁡[B​s​t​u​c​k]=𝔼⁡[WB]/n=O⁡(B)\mathbb{E}[B_{\emph{stuck}}]=\mathbb{E}[W^{B}]/n=O(\sqrt{B}), so the normalized throughput loss in the embedded review process is O(B−1/2)O(B^{-1/2}). The same bound applies to every prefix b≤Bb\leq B, and therefore

1B​∑b=1B𝔼⁡[Wb]≤1B​∑b=1BO⁡(b)=O⁡(B).\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbb{E}[W^{b}]\leq\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}O(\sqrt{b})=O(\sqrt{B}).

This time-averaged backlog bound is the quantity used for the latency and TTFT estimates.

Scaling with the horizon.

Let Δπ\Delta^{\pi} denote the fixed processing time of a threshold-sized batch under policy π\pi. In the scaled system, the corresponding processing time is Δπ/ζ\Delta^{\pi}/\zeta. Over a calendar horizon TT, set

Bζ=⌊ζ​TΔπ⌋.B_{\zeta}=\left\lfloor\frac{\zeta T}{\Delta^{\pi}}\right\rfloor.

Then Bζ=ζ​T/Δπ+O⁡(1)B_{\zeta}=\zeta T/\Delta^{\pi}+O(1). The terminal backlog bound gives normalized throughput loss O(Bζ−1/2)=O((ζT)−1/2)O(B_{\zeta}^{-1/2})=O((\zeta T)^{-1/2}). For delay, the theorem reports service-normalized time, so one scaled threshold-batch interval has length Δπ\Delta^{\pi}; the time-averaged backlog bound therefore gives latency and TTFT contributions O⁡(Bζ1/2)=O⁡((ζ​T)1/2)O(B_{\zeta}^{1/2})=O((\zeta T)^{1/2}). The bounded number of service stages is lower order. The event-driven WAIT clock is connected to this review-process calculation by the cumulative service-opportunity coupling below, which includes the single-type case as m=1m=1.

D.0.2 Multiple-Type Case

We now extend to mm known output-length classes. The additional issue is that event-driven WAIT need not process the full class composition in every realized batch: if only a subset of class queues has reached its threshold, only that subset is batched. The proof handles this by introducing an auxiliary embedded full-threshold process observed at deterministic review epochs. The actual policy is the event-driven WAIT policy from the main text, which batches all currently eligible types whenever the server becomes idle. The embedded process is not used to compare the total number of realized batches or the total fixed overhead paid by the two systems. Its role is to put each type-jj threshold queue on a common full-threshold service scale, obtain a Lindley-type recursion, and then transfer the resulting bounds back to the actual policy through a sample path coupling of service opportunities.

For a threshold vector π=[n1,…,nm]\pi=[n_{1},\ldots,n_{m}], let

Δπ≡Δ​T[1,…,m]=d0+d1​Mπ,Mπ=∑j=1mnj​(lj′+1)​(lj+lj′2).\Delta^{\pi}\equiv\Delta T_{[1,\ldots,m]}=d_{0}+d_{1}M^{\pi},\qquad M^{\pi}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}n_{j}(l_{j}^{\prime}+1)\left(l_{j}+\frac{l_{j}^{\prime}}{2}\right). (18)

This is the processing time of the full threshold composition, i.e., the batch that contains njn_{j} prompts from every decode stage of every type jj. The load-balance and memory conditions are

λj​Δπ≤njfor all ​j∈[m],\displaystyle\lambda_{j}\Delta^{\pi}\leq n_{j}\quad\text{for all }j\in[m], (19)
M∗≤Mπ≤C.\displaystyle M^{*}\leq M^{\pi}\leq C.

The first line says that, over one full-threshold iteration, the expected type-jj arrivals do not exceed the njn_{j} type-jj prompts that can be advanced from each active stage. The second line is the corresponding feasibility condition: the threshold composition is at least on the scale of the fluid memory requirement but does not exceed the physical memory CC.

Lemma 15 (GPU-resident memory invariant).

Starting from the empty system, WAIT maintains

Nj​s(t)≤nj,j∈[m],s=1,…,lj′,N_{js}(t)\leq n_{j},\qquad j\in[m],\;s=1,\ldots,l_{j}^{\prime},

where Nj​s​(t)N_{js}(t) is the number of resident type-jj prompts at decode stage ss. Stage-0 prompts that have not been selected for prefill have no resident KV cache.

The proof is by induction over batch completions. If type jj is not served in a realized batch, its GPU-resident prompts at decode stages are unchanged. If type jj is served, the invariant before the batch implies that each decode stage contains at most njn_{j} prompts, so WAIT selects all prompts currently present in that stage. After the batch completes, stage s+1s+1 contains only the prompts advanced from stage ss, again at most njn_{j}. Thus no decode stage can exceed njn_{j} resident prompts.

The invariant gives the memory-feasibility statement needed by the policy. If aj​0​(t)≤nja_{j0}(t)\leq n_{j} denotes the number of type-jj prompts selected for prefill in the current batch, then at any decision epoch,

∑j=1m∑s=1lj′Nj​s​(t)​(lj+s)+∑j=1maj​0​(t)​lj≤∑j=1mnj​∑s=0lj′(lj+s)=Mπ≤C.\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{s=1}^{l_{j}^{\prime}}N_{js}(t)(l_{j}+s)+\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j0}(t)l_{j}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{m}n_{j}\sum_{s=0}^{l_{j}^{\prime}}(l_{j}+s)=M^{\pi}\leq C.

Thus unselected resident prompts are included in the memory accounting, while unselected stage-0 prompts remain outside the GPU KV-cache state. The same bound holds after the simultaneous completion update: selected stage-ss prompts replace selected stage-s+1s+1 prompts, while final-stage prompts complete and release memory. Thus the invariant is checked consistently at launch epochs, during the selected batch, and after the batch-completion transition.

For any realized event-driven WAIT batch rr, let aj​s(r)≤nja^{(r)}_{js}\leq n_{j} be the number of selected type-jj prompts at decode stage ss, and let JrJ_{r} be the set of selected types. The selected batch composition has size

Mr=∑j∈Jr∑s=0lj′aj​s(r)​(lj+s)≤∑j=1mnj​∑s=0lj′(lj+s)=Mπ.M_{r}=\sum_{j\in J_{r}}\sum_{s=0}^{l_{j}^{\prime}}a^{(r)}_{js}(l_{j}+s)\leq\sum_{j=1}^{m}n_{j}\sum_{s=0}^{l_{j}^{\prime}}(l_{j}+s)=M^{\pi}.

Therefore the physical processing time of the realized batch in the ζ\zeta-scaled system is

Sr(ζ)=d0+d1​Mrζ≤Δπζ.S_{r}^{(\zeta)}=\frac{d_{0}+d_{1}M_{r}}{\zeta}\leq\frac{\Delta^{\pi}}{\zeta}.

This bound concerns processing time, while Lemma 15 gives memory feasibility. Actual batches may contain fewer types and have shorter duration, but no realized WAIT batch is larger than the full-threshold composition. The fixed overhead d0d_{0} is therefore handled through a calendar-time coupling of cumulative service opportunities, not by matching realized batches one for one. If several same-type threshold batches accumulate during one busy period, later same-type batches may wait behind earlier same-type batches. The coupling below therefore compares cumulative type-wise service counts at deterministic review epochs.

In the ζ\zeta-scaled system, one full-threshold review interval has physical length Δπ/ζ\Delta^{\pi}/\zeta. Define deterministic review epochs

ub=bΔπ/ζ,b=0,1,2,….u_{b}=b\Delta^{\pi}/\zeta,\qquad b=0,1,2,\ldots.

The embedded process reviews the entry queues only at these epochs. We use an end-of-interval accounting convention: arrivals accumulate over (ub,ub+1](u_{b},u_{b+1}], and at ub+1u_{b+1} the embedded process removes one type-jj entry batch of size njn_{j} whenever the type-jj entry queue has reached njn_{j}. The corresponding type-jj service opportunity also advances up to njn_{j} resident type-jj prompts from each active decode stage. Equivalently, one can view the selected work as occupying the following full review interval. A batch removed at review ub+1u_{b+1} can therefore shift completion accounting by at most lj′+1l_{j}^{\prime}+1 embedded intervals for type jj, which contributes only O⁡((ζ​T)−1)O((\zeta T)^{-1}) to normalized throughput and O⁡(1)O(1) to service-normalized average delay. The full-threshold interval length is feasible by the resident memory invariant above, and it is deliberately chosen as the service scale at which the type-wise threshold queues have Lindley recursions.

Throughout this argument, bb indexes embedded full-threshold review intervals, not realized event-driven WAIT batches.

Lemma 16 (Type-wise sample path coupling of service opportunities).

Couple actual event-driven WAIT and the auxiliary embedded full-threshold process on the same arrival sample path, both starting empty. Let Lζ=Δπ/ζL_{\zeta}=\Delta^{\pi}/\zeta and ub=b​Lζu_{b}=bL_{\zeta}. For type jj, let Rjπ​(t)R_{j}^{\pi}(t) be the cumulative number of type-jj threshold batches of size njn_{j} started by actual WAIT by time tt, and let Rjπ¯​(b)R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b) be the cumulative number of type-jj batches removed from the embedded entry queue at reviews u1,…,ubu_{1},\ldots,u_{b}. Then

Rjπ​(ub+1)≥Rjπ¯​(b),b≥0,j∈[m].R_{j}^{\pi}(u_{b+1})\geq R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b),\qquad b\geq 0,\;j\in[m].

For downstream stages, each corresponding one-stage advancement has the same start-count lag and completes within one additional full-threshold interval.

To prove the entry-batch dominance, fix a type jj and define the actual type-jj entry residual

Qjπ(t)=Aj(0,t]−njRjπ(t).Q_{j}^{\pi}(t)=A_{j}(0,t]-n_{j}R_{j}^{\pi}(t).

This identity follows because actual WAIT removes exactly one type-jj entry threshold group whenever it launches a batch containing type jj. We prove

Rjπ​(ub+1)≥Rjπ¯​(b)R_{j}^{\pi}(u_{b+1})\geq R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b)

by induction on bb. The claim is trivial for b=0b=0. Assume Rjπ​(ub)≥Rjπ¯​(b−1)R_{j}^{\pi}(u_{b})\geq R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b-1). If the embedded process does not remove a type-jj entry batch at review ubu_{b}, then Rjπ¯​(b)=Rjπ¯​(b−1)R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b)=R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b-1), and the induction hypothesis and monotonicity of RjπR_{j}^{\pi} give the claim. Suppose instead that the embedded process removes one type-jj entry batch at ubu_{b}. If Rjπ​(ub)≥Rjπ¯​(b)R_{j}^{\pi}(u_{b})\geq R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b), the claim again follows by monotonicity. Otherwise, since all counts are integer and Rjπ¯​(b)=Rjπ¯​(b−1)+1R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b)=R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b-1)+1, the induction hypothesis implies

Rjπ​(ub)=Rjπ¯​(b−1).R_{j}^{\pi}(u_{b})=R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b-1).

The embedded removal at ubu_{b} means

Aj(0,ub]−njRjπ¯(b−1)≥nj.A_{j}(0,u_{b}]-n_{j}R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b-1)\geq n_{j}.

Therefore Qjπ​(ub)≥njQ_{j}^{\pi}(u_{b})\geq n_{j}, so type jj is eligible in the actual system at time ubu_{b}. If the server is idle, WAIT starts a batch including type jj immediately. If the server is busy, the current realized batch completes by ub+1u_{b+1}, because every realized batch has duration at most LζL_{\zeta}, and the next WAIT launch includes all eligible types, including jj, unless type jj has already been served. Hence

Rjπ​(ub+1)≥Rjπ¯​(b).R_{j}^{\pi}(u_{b+1})\geq R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b).

This proves the cumulative dominance without asserting that each individual same-type threshold batch starts within one full-threshold interval of its own eligibility time. The argument is in calendar time and includes the fixed overhead paid by any subset batch.

The stage-advancement statement follows from the same sample path coupling of service opportunities, with completed one-stage advancements rather than entry starts as the induction variable. A type-jj service opportunity that starts by ub+1u_{b+1} completes no later than ub+2u_{b+2}, because its processing time is at most one full-threshold interval. Each such opportunity advances up to njn_{j} prompts from every active type-jj stage. Propagating the cumulative dominance stage by stage gives only a type-dependent constant review-interval lag across the fixed lj′l_{j}^{\prime} downstream stages. Equivalently, if Rj​sπ​(t)R_{js}^{\pi}(t) and Rj​sπ¯​(b)R_{js}^{\bar{\pi}}(b) count completed type-jj advancements from stage ss to s+1s+1 in the actual and embedded systems, then for each fixed jj and ss there is a constant cj​sc_{js}, depending only on lj′l_{j}^{\prime}, such that

Rj​sπ​(ub+cj​s)≥Rj​sπ¯​(b).R_{js}^{\pi}(u_{b+c_{js}})\geq R_{js}^{\bar{\pi}}(b).

For the delay conversion, the same coupling gives an entry-queue area comparison. For t∈(ub,ub+1]t\in(u_{b},u_{b+1}], the case b=0b=0 is immediate, and for b≥1b\geq 1, Lemma 16 gives Rjπ​(t)≥Rjπ​(ub)≥Rjπ¯​(b−1)R_{j}^{\pi}(t)\geq R_{j}^{\pi}(u_{b})\geq R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b-1). Since

Aj(0,ub]−njRjπ¯(b−1)≤W¯(j)b+nj,A_{j}(0,u_{b}]-n_{j}R_{j}^{\bar{\pi}}(b-1)\leq\bar{W}^{b}_{(j)}+n_{j},

we have

Qjπ(t)≤W¯(j)b+nj+Aj(ub,ub+1].Q_{j}^{\pi}(t)\leq\bar{W}^{b}_{(j)}+n_{j}+A_{j}(u_{b},u_{b+1}].

Therefore, for any BB,

𝔼⁡[ζ​∫0uBQjπ​(t)​𝑑t]≤Δπ​∑b=0B−1𝔼⁡[W¯(j)b]+O⁡(B).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\zeta\int_{0}^{u_{B}}Q_{j}^{\pi}(t)\,dt\right]\leq\Delta^{\pi}\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\mathbb{E}[\bar{W}^{b}_{(j)}]+O(B).

Lemma 16 is the structural step that transfers the embedded-process queue bounds back to event-driven WAIT. It does not require the actual system to use fewer batches than the embedded process. Actual WAIT may realize different subset compositions across time, and same-type threshold batches can accumulate during a busy period, but the cumulative type-wise removals of the embedded process are matched by actual type-wise service opportunities with a constant review-interval lag. Thus it is enough to bound the embedded comparison queues: the constant lag and the bounded in-service pipeline contribute only O⁡((ζ​T)−1)O((\zeta T)^{-1}) to normalized throughput and O⁡(1)O(1) to the service-normalized delay metrics.

For the embedded process, let W¯(j)b\bar{W}^{b}_{(j)} be the residual type-jj entry queue after the bb-th review, and let

X¯(j)b=Aj(ub,ub+1]∼Poisson(ζλjΔπζ)=Poisson(λjΔπ).\bar{X}^{b}_{(j)}=A_{j}(u_{b},u_{b+1}]\sim\text{Poisson}\!\left(\zeta\lambda_{j}\frac{\Delta^{\pi}}{\zeta}\right)=\text{Poisson}(\lambda_{j}\Delta^{\pi}).

The arrivals {X¯(j)b}\{\bar{X}^{b}_{(j)}\} are independent across embedded intervals and do not depend on other type queues. With the end-of-interval accounting convention above, the residual entry queue evolves as

W¯(j)b+1=W¯(j)b+X¯(j)b−nj 1{W¯(j)b+X¯(j)b≥nj}.\bar{W}^{b+1}_{(j)}=\bar{W}^{b}_{(j)}+\bar{X}^{b}_{(j)}-n_{j}\,\mathbf{1}\{\bar{W}^{b}_{(j)}+\bar{X}^{b}_{(j)}\geq n_{j}\}.

This is the point at which the batch-composition issue is reduced to a stochastic comparison: the only coupling across types is the deterministic feasibility condition Mπ≤CM^{\pi}\leq C, while the embedded process gives each type its own threshold queue.

Lemma 17 (Embedded comparison queue bound).

For each type jj, define

W~(j)0=2​nj,W~(j)b+1=max⁡{2​nj,W~(j)b+X¯(j)b−nj}.\widetilde{W}_{(j)}^{0}=2n_{j},\qquad\widetilde{W}_{(j)}^{b+1}=\max\{2n_{j},\widetilde{W}_{(j)}^{b}+\bar{X}^{b}_{(j)}-n_{j}\}.

Then W~(j)b≥W¯(j)b\widetilde{W}^{b}_{(j)}\geq\bar{W}^{b}_{(j)} for all b≥0b\geq 0 and j∈[m]j\in[m].

The proof is in Appendix G.3. Let μj=λj​Δπ\mu_{j}=\lambda_{j}\Delta^{\pi}. The increment in the dominating process is X¯(j)b−nj\bar{X}^{b}_{(j)}-n_{j}, whose mean is μj−nj≤0\mu_{j}-n_{j}\leq 0 by (19). If μj=nj\mu_{j}=n_{j}, the same random-walk maximum argument used in the single-type proof gives

𝔼⁡[W¯(j)B]≤𝔼⁡[W~(j)B]=O⁡(B1/2).\mathbb{E}[\bar{W}^{B}_{(j)}]\leq\mathbb{E}[\widetilde{W}^{B}_{(j)}]=O(B^{1/2}).

The same bound holds for every prefix b≤Bb\leq B, so

1B​∑b=0B−1𝔼⁡[W¯(j)b]=O⁡(B1/2).\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\mathbb{E}[\bar{W}^{b}_{(j)}]=O(B^{1/2}).

If μj<nj\mu_{j}<n_{j}, the dominating process has strictly negative drift. Since

|𝔼⁡[X¯(j)b−nj]|=nj−μj,\left|\mathbb{E}[\bar{X}^{b}_{(j)}-n_{j}]\right|=n_{j}-\mu_{j},

by Kingman’s bound (Kingman, 1962):

supB≥0𝔼⁡[W¯(j)B]≤2​nj+𝔼⁡[(X¯(j)b−nj)2]2​(nj−μj)<∞.\sup_{B\geq 0}\mathbb{E}[\bar{W}^{B}_{(j)}]\leq 2n_{j}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\bar{X}^{b}_{(j)}-n_{j})^{2}]}{2(n_{j}-\mu_{j})}<\infty.

Combining the zero-drift and negative-drift cases, under the nonpositive drift condition in (19),

∑j=1m𝔼⁡[W¯(j)B]=O⁡(B1/2),1B​∑b=0B−1∑j=1m𝔼⁡[W¯(j)b]=O⁡(B1/2).\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}[\bar{W}^{B}_{(j)}]=O(B^{1/2}),\qquad\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=0}^{B-1}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}[\bar{W}^{b}_{(j)}]=O(B^{1/2}).

Under strict slack μj<nj\mu_{j}<n_{j} for all jj, both quantities are O⁡(1)O(1). If equality holds for at least one type and strict inequality holds for the others, the zero-drift types dominate the aggregate bounds, so the first part of the theorem applies. Types with zero arrival rates can be omitted from [m][m].

It remains to translate these BB-interval bounds into the theorem’s finite-horizon metrics. The terminal queue bound and the prefix-average queue bound play different roles: the former controls missed completions at the horizon, while the latter controls accumulated waiting. The number of completed embedded full-threshold intervals in the physical horizon [0,T][0,T] is exactly

Bζ​(T)=max⁡{b:ub≤T}=⌊ζ​TΔπ⌋,B_{\zeta}(T)=\max\{b:u_{b}\leq T\}=\left\lfloor\frac{\zeta T}{\Delta^{\pi}}\right\rfloor,

and the residual time is less than one embedded full-threshold interval. This is the number of deterministic review intervals in the embedded process, not the number of actual event-driven WAIT batches. Since Bζ=ζ​T/Δπ+O⁡(1)B_{\zeta}=\zeta T/\Delta^{\pi}+O(1), Bζ−1/2=O((ζT)−1/2)B_{\zeta}^{-1/2}=O((\zeta T)^{-1/2}) and Bζ−1=O⁡((ζ​T)−1)B_{\zeta}^{-1}=O((\zeta T)^{-1}).

For throughput, the terminal entry backlog controls the completion shortfall. More precisely, for the embedded process,

Throughput∗−𝔼[Throughput(ζ,π¯)]≤1ζ​T∑j=1mlj′𝔼[W¯(j)Bζ+Aj(uBζ,T]+(lj′+2)nj].\textbf{Throughput}^{*}-\mathbb{E}[\textbf{Throughput}^{(\zeta,\bar{\pi})}]\leq\frac{1}{\zeta T}\sum_{j=1}^{m}l_{j}^{\prime}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bar{W}^{B_{\zeta}}_{(j)}+A_{j}(u_{B_{\zeta}},T]+(l_{j}^{\prime}+2)n_{j}\right].

The second term accounts for final partial-interval arrivals, and the last term absorbs the bounded in-service pipeline, startup effects, and the one-interval lag from Lemma 16. Since T−uBζ<Δπ/ζT-u_{B_{\zeta}}<\Delta^{\pi}/\zeta, 𝔼[Aj(uBζ,T]]≤λjΔπ=O(1)\mathbb{E}[A_{j}(u_{B_{\zeta}},T]]\leq\lambda_{j}\Delta^{\pi}=O(1). Thus the terminal-backlog term gives an O((ζT)−1/2)O((\zeta T)^{-1/2}) gap under nonpositive drift and an O⁡((ζ​T)−1)O((\zeta T)^{-1}) gap under strict slack.

For delay, we use the prefix-average queue bound instead. Let Q¯b=∑j=1mW¯(j)b\bar{Q}^{b}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\bar{W}^{b}_{(j)}. In physical time, each embedded full-threshold interval has length Δπ/ζ\Delta^{\pi}/\zeta. The theorem, however, reports service-normalized delay, multiplying elapsed physical time by ζ\zeta. Thus each embedded interval contributes a constant scaled time Δπ\Delta^{\pi}. The entry-area comparison above gives

𝔼⁡[ζ​∫0T∑j=1mQjπ​(t)​𝑑t]≤Δπ​∑b=0Bζ−1𝔼⁡[Q¯b]+O⁡(Bζ),\mathbb{E}\!\left[\zeta\int_{0}^{T}\sum_{j=1}^{m}Q_{j}^{\pi}(t)\,dt\right]\leq\Delta^{\pi}\sum_{b=0}^{B_{\zeta}-1}\mathbb{E}[\bar{Q}^{b}]+O(B_{\zeta}),

where the O⁡(Bζ)O(B_{\zeta}) term includes final partial intervals and the expected arrivals inside each review interval. The remaining latency contribution comes from prompts that have already entered the GPU-resident pipeline. This part is uniformly bounded in area: by Lemma 15,

ζ​∫0T∑j=1m∑s=1lj′Nj​s​(t)​𝑑t≤ζ​T​∑j=1mnj​lj′=O⁡(Bζ).\zeta\int_{0}^{T}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\sum_{s=1}^{l_{j}^{\prime}}N_{js}(t)\,dt\leq\zeta T\sum_{j=1}^{m}n_{j}l_{j}^{\prime}=O(B_{\zeta}).

Selected stage-0 prompts currently in prefill service and selected decode prompts currently in service are also bounded by ∑jnj​(lj′+1)\sum_{j}n_{j}(l_{j}^{\prime}+1) at every time, and hence contribute another O⁡(Bζ)O(B_{\zeta}) service-normalized area. Equivalently, after entry admission, the fixed number lj′l_{j}^{\prime} of type-jj stage advancements and the constant review-interval lag in Lemma 16 add only O⁡(1)O(1) to the average service-normalized latency and TTFT. Under the delay convention in Section 2, expected finite-horizon delay is the expected total censored delay divided by the expected number of arrivals, which is Θ⁡(Bζ)\Theta(B_{\zeta}). Therefore

𝔼⁡[Latency(ζ,π)],𝔼⁡[TTFT(ζ,π)]≤O⁡(1Bζ​∑b=0Bζ−1𝔼⁡[Q¯b])+O⁡(1).\mathbb{E}[\textbf{Latency}^{(\zeta,\pi)}],\mathbb{E}[\textbf{TTFT}^{(\zeta,\pi)}]\leq O\!\left(\frac{1}{B_{\zeta}}\sum_{b=0}^{B_{\zeta}-1}\mathbb{E}[\bar{Q}^{b}]\right)+O(1).

The prefix bound gives

𝔼⁡[Latency(ζ,π)],𝔼⁡[TTFT(ζ,π)]=O⁡(Bζ1/2)=O⁡((ζ​T)1/2)\mathbb{E}[\textbf{Latency}^{(\zeta,\pi)}],\mathbb{E}[\textbf{TTFT}^{(\zeta,\pi)}]=O(B_{\zeta}^{1/2})=O((\zeta T)^{1/2})

under nonpositive drift. The corresponding calendar-time delay is smaller by a factor 1/ζ1/\zeta. Under strict slack, the same service-normalized expression is O⁡(1)O(1). Lemma 16 transfers the throughput bound from π¯\bar{\pi} to the actual event-driven WAIT policy, while the delay estimates above use the entry-area and resident-pipeline comparisons directly for actual WAIT. This completes the proof of Theorem 4.

Appendix E Proof of Theorem 7

The proof analyzes Nested WAIT’s threshold dynamics and then shows that the memory condition makes those dynamics feasible with high probability. The main difference from WAIT is that downstream arrivals are generated endogenously: a prompt reaches segment kk only if it survives the boundary lk−1′l_{k-1}^{\prime}. The proof therefore follows the queues at these segment boundaries. Segment 1 is a threshold-renewal queue with external Poisson arrivals. For k≥2k\geq 2, each upstream boundary-crossing opportunity produces a binomially thinned boundary batch. The threshold conditions give negative drift for these embedded queues. Standard reflected-random-walk and exponential-martingale bounds then control their expected size and high-probability excursions; the nonstandard part is the memory accounting that separates fresh boundary arrivals from carryover residual queues.

Let

Λk=∑j=kmλj,pk=ΛkΛk−1,k≥2,\Lambda_{k}=\sum_{j=k}^{m}\lambda_{j},\qquad p_{k}=\frac{\Lambda_{k}}{\Lambda_{k-1}},\quad k\geq 2,

and write

Δπ=Δ​T[1,…,m]​(n1,…,nm)=d0+d1​Mπ.\Delta^{\pi}=\Delta T_{[1,\ldots,m]}(n_{1},\ldots,n_{m})=d_{0}+d_{1}M^{\pi}.

The theorem assumes Λ1​Δπ<n1\Lambda_{1}\Delta^{\pi}<n_{1} and pk<nk/nk−1<1p_{k}<n_{k}/n_{k-1}<1 for k≥2k\geq 2. In the ζ\zeta-scaled system, every realized iteration has physical duration at least d0/ζd_{0}/\zeta, so the number of realized processing opportunities over [0,T][0,T] is at most

Bζmax=⌈ζ​Td0⌉≤1+ζ​Td0.B_{\zeta}^{\max}=\left\lceil\frac{\zeta T}{d_{0}}\right\rceil\leq 1+\frac{\zeta T}{d_{0}}.

This is an upper bound on actual event opportunities, not a full-threshold comparison-slot count.

E.1 Segment-1 Entry Queue

Prompts waiting to enter segment 1 have not been prefilled, so they are outside the GPU-resident KV-cache state. The only subtlety is that the server may idle while waiting for the segment-1 threshold. We therefore index the segment-1 queue by threshold renewals rather than by realized processing iterations. Let RqR_{q} be the residual number of not-yet-prefilled prompts immediately after the qq-th segment-1 service start, after n1n_{1} prompts have been removed for prefill. During the following service period, the number of external arrivals is stochastically dominated by

Y¯(1)q∼Poisson⁡(Λ1​Δπ),\bar{Y}^{q}_{(1)}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\Lambda_{1}\Delta^{\pi}),

because the physical service period is at most Δπ/ζ\Delta^{\pi}/\zeta and arrivals occur at rate ζ​Λ1\zeta\Lambda_{1}. If the residual plus these arrivals is below n1n_{1}, the system idles until the next arrivals complete the threshold and then immediately starts the next segment-1 service. Thus

Rq+1≤(Rq+Y¯(1)q−n1)+.R_{q+1}\leq(R_{q}+\bar{Y}^{q}_{(1)}-n_{1})^{+}.

This recursion is dominated by the reflected random walk

R~(1)0=2​n1,R~(1)q+1=max⁡{2​n1,R~(1)q+Y¯(1)q−n1}.\widetilde{R}^{0}_{(1)}=2n_{1},\qquad\widetilde{R}^{q+1}_{(1)}=\max\{2n_{1},\widetilde{R}^{q}_{(1)}+\bar{Y}^{q}_{(1)}-n_{1}\}.

Since 𝔼⁡[Y¯(1)q]−n1=Λ1​Δπ−n1<0\mathbb{E}[\bar{Y}^{q}_{(1)}]-n_{1}=\Lambda_{1}\Delta^{\pi}-n_{1}<0, the standard Lindley-recursion bound for a random walk with negative drift (Kingman, 1962; Asmussen, 2003, see, e.g.,) gives

supq≥0𝔼⁡[Rq]≤2​n1+𝔼⁡[(Y¯(1)q−n1)2]2​(n1−Λ1​Δπ)<∞.\sup_{q\geq 0}\mathbb{E}[R_{q}]\leq 2n_{1}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\bar{Y}^{q}_{(1)}-n_{1})^{2}]}{2(n_{1}-\Lambda_{1}\Delta^{\pi})}<\infty.

The idle time before the next segment-1 service is the time needed to collect fewer than n1n_{1} arrivals, whose expected physical length is O⁡(1/ζ)O(1/\zeta); in service-normalized time this contributes O⁡(1)O(1).

E.2 Boundary Queues for Downstream Segments

For k≥2k\geq 2, consider an opportunity at which segment k−1k-1 advances prompts across boundary lk−1′l_{k-1}^{\prime}. Let Ak−1r≤nk−1A^{r}_{k-1}\leq n_{k-1} be the number of prompts that cross this boundary at the rr-th such opportunity. Conditional on the filtration just before output-length revelation at the boundary, the indicators that these prompts continue to segment kk are independent Bernoulli random variables with probability pk=Λk/Λk−1p_{k}=\Lambda_{k}/\Lambda_{k-1}. This uses the i.i.d. output-length mix and the fact that service before the boundary is nonanticipating with respect to future output length; before a boundary is reached, prompts with possible remaining output-length classes are exchangeable within the surviving mixture. Therefore

Y(k)r∣Ak−1r∼Binomial(Ak−1r,pk),Y(k)r⪯Y¯(k)r,Y^{r}_{(k)}\mid A^{r}_{k-1}\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(A^{r}_{k-1},p_{k}),\qquad Y^{r}_{(k)}\preceq\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)},

where the dominating variables Y¯(k)r∼Binomial⁡(nk−1,pk)\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n_{k-1},p_{k}) can be chosen independent across boundary opportunities.

Let V(k)rV^{r}_{(k)} be the carryover boundary queue at stage lk−1′l_{k-1}^{\prime} after the threshold review at the start of the rr-th opportunity in which segment k−1k-1 is processed. Thus V(k)rV^{r}_{(k)} is a post-review residual, not the pre-review boundary population. This convention preserves the nested, prefix structure of the algorithm. Whenever segment k−1k-1 is active, all earlier segment thresholds have been met. If the boundary queue for segment kk also contains at least nkn_{k} prompts at that review, Nested WAIT includes segment kk in the same prefix batch and removes a threshold batch from the boundary. During the batch, at most Ak−1r≤nk−1A^{r}_{k-1}\leq n_{k-1} additional prompts may survive segment k−1k-1 and join the boundary. These fresh survivors are part of the just-processed upstream threshold batch, so their KV-cache memory is charged to the threshold-sized batch term MπM^{\pi}. Only the carryover residual remains as additional boundary memory. With the binomial domination above, the pre-review queue for the next opportunity is V(k)r+Y¯(k)rV^{r}_{(k)}+\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}, and the post-review residual satisfies

V(k)r+1≤V(k)r+Y¯(k)r−nk𝟏{V(k)r+Y¯(k)r≥nk}.V^{r+1}_{(k)}\leq V^{r}_{(k)}+\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}-n_{k}{\bf 1}\{V^{r}_{(k)}+\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}\geq n_{k}\}.

The residual queue is dominated by

W~(k)0=nk,W~(k)r+1=max⁡{nk,W~(k)r+Y¯(k)r−nk}.\widetilde{W}^{0}_{(k)}=n_{k},\qquad\widetilde{W}^{r+1}_{(k)}=\max\{n_{k},\widetilde{W}^{r}_{(k)}+\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}-n_{k}\}.

This domination follows by induction over boundary-crossing opportunities. If V(k)r+Y¯(k)r≥nkV^{r}_{(k)}+\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}\geq n_{k}, the post-review residual is at most V(k)r+Y¯(k)r−nkV^{r}_{(k)}+\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}-n_{k}, which is bounded by W~(k)r+Y¯(k)r−nk\widetilde{W}^{r}_{(k)}+\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}-n_{k}. If V(k)r+Y¯(k)r<nkV^{r}_{(k)}+\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}<n_{k}, the residual is below nkn_{k}, while the dominating recursion is always at least nkn_{k}. Hence V(k)r≤W~(k)rV^{r}_{(k)}\leq\widetilde{W}^{r}_{(k)} for all rr.

The increments Y¯(k)r−nk\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}-n_{k} have strictly negative drift because

𝔼⁡[Y¯(k)r−nk]=nk−1​pk−nk<0.\mathbb{E}[\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}-n_{k}]=n_{k-1}p_{k}-n_{k}<0.

Applying the same negative-drift reflected-random-walk bound yields, uniformly in rr,

𝔼[V(k)r]≤nk+𝔼⁡[(Y¯(k)r−nk)2]2​(nk−nk−1​pk)<∞,k=2,…,m.\mathbb{E}[V^{r}_{(k)}]\leq n_{k}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}-n_{k})^{2}]}{2(n_{k}-n_{k-1}p_{k})}<\infty,\qquad k=2,\ldots,m.

Thus all external and downstream boundary queues have bounded expected size, uniformly over ζ\zeta and TT.

We also use the stage-cap invariant induced by the threshold rule. Starting from the empty system, every threshold-controlled interior stage of segment kk contains at most nkn_{k} resident prompts. A batch that includes segment kk advances at most nkn_{k} prompts from each preceding stage into the next stage; a batch that excludes segment kk leaves its interior stages unchanged. The only resident queues not covered by this interior-stage cap are the downstream boundary queues V(k)V_{(k)}, k≥2k\geq 2, which are controlled by the residual-queue bounds above.

E.3 Throughput and Delay

We first translate the queue bounds into performance estimates for the threshold-controlled dynamics before memory repair is invoked. Let W(1)​(T)W_{(1)}(T) denote the segment-1 entry residual at time TT, let V(k)​(T)V_{(k)}(T) be the downstream resident boundary queue for k≥2k\geq 2, and let Ik​(T)I_{k}(T) be the number of prompts inside the threshold-controlled interior of segment kk. There are constants αk,βk\alpha_{k},\beta_{k}, depending only on the fixed output lengths, such that terminal unfinished decode work is bounded by

∑k=1mαk​W(k)​(T)+∑k=1mβk​Ik​(T)+Atail​(T),\sum_{k=1}^{m}\alpha_{k}W_{(k)}(T)+\sum_{k=1}^{m}\beta_{k}I_{k}(T)+A_{\mathrm{tail}}(T),

Throughput∗−𝔼⁡[Throughput(ζ,π)]\displaystyle\textbf{Throughput}^{*}-\mathbb{E}[\textbf{Throughput}^{(\zeta,\pi)}] ≤1ζ​T​𝔼​[∑k=1mαk​W(k)​(T)+∑k=1mβk​Ik​(T)+Atail​(T)]\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\zeta T}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_{k=1}^{m}\alpha_{k}W_{(k)}(T)+\sum_{k=1}^{m}\beta_{k}I_{k}(T)+A_{\mathrm{tail}}(T)\right]
=O⁡((ζ​T)−1).\displaystyle=O((\zeta T)^{-1}).

For delay, let Q⁡(t)Q(t) be the total number of prompts in the segment-1 entry queue, downstream boundary queues, and threshold-controlled segment interiors. The bounds above, together with the O⁡(1/ζ)O(1/\zeta) expected idle period needed to collect fewer than a threshold batch, imply

𝔼⁡[∫0TQ⁡(t)​𝑑t]=O⁡(T).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}Q(t)\,dt\right]=O(T).

The expected number of arrivals over [0,T][0,T] is ζ​Λ1​T=Θ⁡(ζ​T)\zeta\Lambda_{1}T=\Theta(\zeta T). Hence the calendar-time censored average latency and TTFT are O⁡(1/ζ)O(1/\zeta). The theorem reports service-normalized delays, Latency(ζ,π)=ζ​Latencycal(ζ,π)\textbf{Latency}^{(\zeta,\pi)}=\zeta\textbf{Latency}_{\rm cal}^{(\zeta,\pi)} and TTFT(ζ,π)=ζ​TTFTcal(ζ,π)\textbf{TTFT}^{(\zeta,\pi)}=\zeta\textbf{TTFT}_{\rm cal}^{(\zeta,\pi)}, so

𝔼⁡[Latency(ζ,π)],𝔼⁡[TTFT(ζ,π)]=O⁡(1).\mathbb{E}[\textbf{Latency}^{(\zeta,\pi)}],\mathbb{E}[\textbf{TTFT}^{(\zeta,\pi)}]=O(1).

E.4 High-Probability Memory Bound

The base term

Mπ=∑k=1mnk​(l+s¯k)​δkM^{\pi}=\sum_{k=1}^{m}n_{k}(l+\bar{s}_{k})\delta_{k}

accounts for threshold-sized segment batches. With the convention used in Theorem 7, segment 1 covers stages s=0,…,l1′s=0,\ldots,l_{1}^{\prime}, while for k≥2k\geq 2, the resident boundary queue at s=lk−1′s=l_{k-1}^{\prime} is tracked separately and segment kk’s interior covers s=lk−1′+1,…,lk′s=l_{k-1}^{\prime}+1,\ldots,l_{k}^{\prime}. The memory accounting separates two boundary terms. Fresh survivors that have just crossed from segment k−1k-1 are a subset of the upstream threshold batch. They have the same KV-cache size as the prompts charged to the s=lk−1′s=l_{k-1}^{\prime} stage of segment k−1k-1 in MπM^{\pi}, so charging them to the base term does not add memory. The only additional memory is the carryover residual left at downstream boundaries across opportunities. Therefore, if V(k)r≤ckV^{r}_{(k)}\leq c_{k} for all downstream boundaries, then total resident KV-cache memory is at most

Mπ+∑k=2m(l+lk−1′)​ck.M^{\pi}+\sum_{k=2}^{m}(l+l_{k-1}^{\prime})c_{k}.

The deterministic nkn_{k} component of ckc_{k} is on the same scale as the base term: since nk<nk−1n_{k}<n_{k-1}, (l+lk−1′)​nk(l+l_{k-1}^{\prime})n_{k} is bounded by the contribution of the terminal stage s=lk−1′s=l_{k-1}^{\prime} of segment k−1k-1 already included in MπM^{\pi}.

Fix k≥2k\geq 2. Since pk<nk/nk−1<1p_{k}<n_{k}/n_{k-1}<1, Appendix G.5 records the standard exponential-martingale construction for binomial increments and gives a unique θk>0\theta_{k}>0 satisfying

e−θk​nk​(1−pk+pk​eθk)nk−1=1.e^{-\theta_{k}n_{k}}(1-p_{k}+p_{k}e^{\theta_{k}})^{n_{k-1}}=1.

For S(k)i=∑r=1i(Y¯(k)r−nk)S^{i}_{(k)}=\sum_{r=1}^{i}(\bar{Y}^{r}_{(k)}-n_{k}), the process eθk​S(k)ie^{\theta_{k}S^{i}_{(k)}} is a martingale. Doob’s maximal inequality (Durrett, 2019, see, e.g.,) gives

ℙ⁡(max0≤i≤r⁡S(k)i≥x)≤e−θk​x.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\max_{0\leq i\leq r}S^{i}_{(k)}\geq x\right)\leq e^{-\theta_{k}x}.

Equivalently, the finite-horizon reflected-random-walk bound in Appendix G.5 gives, for the dominating boundary queue,

ℙ⁡(max0≤r≤B⁡(W~(k)r−nk)≥x)≤B​e−θk​x,B≥1.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\max_{0\leq r\leq B}\big(\widetilde{W}^{r}_{(k)}-n_{k}\big)\geq x\right)\leq Be^{-\theta_{k}x},\qquad B\geq 1.

Since V(k)r≤W~(k)rV^{r}_{(k)}\leq\widetilde{W}^{r}_{(k)}, set

ck=nk+θk−1​ln⁡(m⁡(1+ζ​T/d0)δ).c_{k}=n_{k}+\theta_{k}^{-1}\ln\!\left(\frac{m(1+\zeta T/d_{0})}{\delta}\right).

Applying this finite-horizon bound with B=BζmaxB=B_{\zeta}^{\max}, and then unioning over k=2,…,mk=2,\ldots,m, gives

ℙ(V(k)r≤ck for all k=2,…,m,r≤Bζmax)≥1−δ.\mathbb{P}\!\left(V^{r}_{(k)}\leq c_{k}\text{ for all }k=2,\ldots,m,\;r\leq B_{\zeta}^{\max}\right)\geq 1-\delta.

Let ℰ\mathcal{E} denote the event in the preceding display. Couple the finite-memory Nested WAIT implementation and the threshold-controlled dynamics analyzed above on the same arrivals and continuation marks until the first time memory repair would be invoked. On ℰ\mathcal{E}, the resident memory after every projected transition is at most Mreq(ζ,π)≤CM_{\mathrm{req}}^{(\zeta,\pi)}\leq C, and actual boundary completions can only reduce the projected memory. The same accounting covers both memory-repair sites in Algorithm 2 and its full event-driven version, Algorithm H.1: after completion updates, repair is allowed only from resident boundary queues, and before launch, repair is allowed only from unselected resident boundary prompts in the conservative projected state Q+Q^{+}.

For the completion-update repair site, fresh survivors occupy slots already charged in MπM^{\pi}, and only carryover resident boundary residuals require the ckc_{k} buffers. Under the stage-cap invariant, all non-boundary resident prompts are covered by the base term MπM^{\pi}; hence on ℰ\mathcal{E}, the post-completion resident memory is already at most Mreq(ζ,π)≤CM_{\mathrm{req}}^{(\zeta,\pi)}\leq C. For the before-launch repair site, the selected boundary prompts are charged to the first interior stage of their next segment in the projected state Q+Q^{+}, again within the base term. The only projected memory outside this base accounting comes from unselected resident boundary prompts, and these are exactly the residual queues controlled by the ckc_{k} buffers on ℰ\mathcal{E}. Thus the projected memory before launch is also at most Mreq(ζ,π)≤CM_{\mathrm{req}}^{(\zeta,\pi)}\leq C. Consequently, on ℰ\mathcal{E}, the repair conditions are never met at either repair site. The within-set eviction order is therefore immaterial on ℰ\mathcal{E}, and this argument makes no recovery claim on ℰc\mathcal{E}^{c}. Hence memory repair is never invoked, the two sample paths coincide on [0,T][0,T], and

ℙ⁡(a memory-overflow-induced eviction occurs over ​[0,T])≤ℙ⁡(ℰc)≤δ.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\text{a memory-overflow-induced eviction occurs over }[0,T]\right)\leq\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}^{c})\leq\delta.

We also record the deterministic no-stall property of Nested WAIT’s restricted repair rule under the theorem’s memory assumption, in particular C≥MπC\geq M^{\pi}. The global LIFO pathology in which late-stage resident prompts remain on the GPU while newly accumulated early-stage prompts are repeatedly evicted cannot occur here. Memory repair never evicts the external queue Q1,0Q_{1,0} and never evicts segment-interior prompts. It only evicts resident boundary prompts, and before launch it evicts only unselected resident boundary prompts in the projected state. By the stage-cap invariant, if all resident boundary prompts eligible for the relevant repair loop have been removed, the remaining resident memory is covered by the base threshold allocation Mπ≤CM^{\pi}\leq C. Thus each repair loop terminates with a feasible state. Moreover, between launches of segment 1, Q1,0Q_{1,0} is not reduced by repair and can only grow through exogenous arrivals and restarted boundary prompts. Hence, once the server is idle and Q1,0≥n1Q_{1,0}\geq n_{1}, the threshold review finds a nonempty prefix and memory repair cannot remove the segment-1 threshold batch; the projected before-launch repair can remove only unselected downstream boundary prompts. If the server is idle and Q1,0<n1Q_{1,0}<n_{1}, then it is waiting for exogenous arrivals rather than resident-memory repair, and since Λ1>0\Lambda_{1}>0, the threshold is reached almost surely in finite time on the continuing arrival process. This is the point where Nested WAIT’s resident-boundary repair rule differs from a generic LIFO rule.

It remains to bound the contribution of ℰc\mathcal{E}^{c} to the unconditional finite-horizon performance metrics. On ℰc\mathcal{E}^{c}, the finite-memory implementation may experience evictions and restarts, so it is no longer coupled to the threshold dynamics analyzed above. The deterministic no-stall property rules out a global memory-induced launch blockade at segment 1, but it does not by itself give the sharp threshold-dynamics queue bounds after restarts or for downstream segments. We therefore charge the entire post-failure contribution using pathwise finite-horizon caps. Each request that arrived before TT contributes at most TT calendar time to latency or TTFT, and realized effective throughput remains nonnegative. Evicted prompts are not counted as new exogenous arrivals; returning them to Q1,0Q_{1,0} can only affect the finite-horizon path after the failure event, whose contribution is bounded by the estimates below. Let ATA_{T} be the total number of external arrivals over [0,T][0,T]. Then AT∼Poisson⁡(μ)A_{T}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu), where μ=ζ​Λ1​T\mu=\zeta\Lambda_{1}T and Λ1=∑j=1mλj\Lambda_{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\lambda_{j}. For any event FF with ℙ⁡(F)≤δ\mathbb{P}(F)\leq\delta,

𝔼[AT𝟏F]≤2μℙ(F)+𝔼[AT𝟏{AT>2μ}]≤2μδ+Cμe−c​μ\mathbb{E}[A_{T}{\bf 1}_{F}]\leq 2\mu\,\mathbb{P}(F)+\mathbb{E}[A_{T}{\bf 1}\{A_{T}>2\mu\}]\leq 2\mu\delta+C\mu e^{-c\mu}

for constants C,c>0C,c>0, using the standard Poisson Chernoff bound. This bound holds for any event FF, with no independence requirement between FF and ATA_{T}. Taking F=ℰcF=\mathcal{E}^{c}, the finite-horizon convention gives a pathwise service-normalized latency or TTFT contribution of at most ζ​T\zeta T per external arrival on ℰc\mathcal{E}^{c}. This uses the convention in Section 2 that expected finite-horizon delay is normalized by the expected number of arrivals, not by the realized arrival count. After normalization by 𝔼⁡[AT]=μ\mathbb{E}[A_{T}]=\mu, the failure-event contribution to either delay metric is at most

ζ​T​𝔼⁡[AT​𝟏ℰc]μ≤ζ​T​(2​δ+C​e−c​μ)=O⁡(1),\zeta T\frac{\mathbb{E}[A_{T}{\bf 1}_{\mathcal{E}^{c}}]}{\mu}\leq\zeta T\left(2\delta+Ce^{-c\mu}\right)=O(1),

because δ≤K​(1+ζ​T)−1\delta\leq K(1+\zeta T)^{-1} and Λ1\Lambda_{1} is fixed.

For throughput, let XTX_{T} be the effective throughput of the threshold-controlled dynamics and let YTY_{T} be the effective throughput of the finite-memory Nested WAIT implementation. Since XT=YTX_{T}=Y_{T} on ℰ\mathcal{E} and YT≥0Y_{T}\geq 0,

Throughput∗−𝔼⁡[YT]≤Throughput∗−𝔼⁡[XT]+𝔼⁡[XT​𝟏ℰc].\textbf{Throughput}^{*}-\mathbb{E}[Y_{T}]\leq\textbf{Throughput}^{*}-\mathbb{E}[X_{T}]+\mathbb{E}[X_{T}{\bf 1}_{\mathcal{E}^{c}}].
