to the normalized throughput gap. Combining these bad-event bounds with the threshold-dynamics estimates above gives the stated unconditional throughput, latency, and TTFT bounds for the finite-memory Nested WAIT implementation.

Finally, Appendix G.5 also gives

θk≥8​(nk−nk−1​pk)nk−1,\theta_{k}\geq\frac{8(n_{k}-n_{k-1}p_{k})}{n_{k-1}},

which is the stated drift-to-buffer scaling. This completes the proof.

Appendix F Proof of Theorem 8

The proof is a conservative version of the Nested WAIT argument. Instead of matching each instantaneous arrival pattern exactly, we dominate each service-window arrival count and each downstream thinning probability by worst-case quantities over the finite horizon. This gives the same bounded-queue and logarithmic-buffer structure as the constant-rate proof. The first-segment waiting condition is used only when converting bounded queues into service-normalized delay bounds; the throughput and memory conclusions use only the upper-side window-load conditions and the finite-horizon safety buffer. The structure proceeds as follows:

  1. 1.

    First segment analysis: Poisson arrivals with time-varying rates are dominated by a time-invariant process using the worst-case scaled-window arrival count Λπ\Lambda^{\pi} from Section A.1. We couple this queue to a Lindley process and apply Kingman’s inequality.

  2. 2.

    Subsequent segments analysis: Poisson-binomial boundary arrivals with time-varying thinning probabilities are pathwise dominated by a binomial process with worst-case continuation probability pk∗p_{k}^{*} defined in Section A.1. The same Lindley coupling then controls each downstream boundary queue.

  3. 3.

    Throughput, delay, and memory: Bounded expected terminal work yields the normalized throughput gap. The service-normalized delay bound additionally uses the first-segment waiting condition to control idle waiting before the first segment. High-probability memory bounds follow from the same martingale construction with worst-case parameters.

We use bb to denote the batch index and k∈{1,…,m}k\in\{1,\ldots,m\} to denote the segment index. The total number of batches is denoted by BB.

F.1 First Segment Analysis

For the first segment (k=1k=1), we use the same threshold-renewal convention as in Appendix E. Idle periods before a segment-1 service start contain fewer than n1n_{1} prompts, so they contribute only a bounded amount of terminal unfinished work and do not affect the memory bound. The first-segment waiting condition in Section A.1 is needed later only to bound these idle periods in service-normalized time. At renewal epochs, the first-segment queue is dominated by the comparison recursion

W(1)b+1=W(1)b+Y(1)b−n1⋅𝟏{W(1)b+Y(1)b≥n1},Y(1)b∼Poisson(∑j=1m𝒜j(ζ)(t(b),ΔTb)),W_{(1)}^{b+1}=W_{(1)}^{b}+Y_{(1)}^{b}-n_{1}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{W_{(1)}^{b}+Y_{(1)}^{b}\geq n_{1}\},\quad Y_{(1)}^{b}\sim\text{Poisson}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathcal{A}_{j}^{(\zeta)}(t(b),\Delta T_{b})\Big),

where t⁡(b)t(b) denotes the physical start time of batch bb and Δ​Tb\Delta T_{b} denotes the service-normalized processing time of that batch, so its physical duration is Δ​Tb/ζ\Delta T_{b}/\zeta. If the actual queue is below threshold, the server waits until enough arrivals occur and then removes n1n_{1}; the displayed recursion is therefore an upper comparison for queue length, not an exact event-time identity.

Worst-case domination.

Time-varying arrival rates prevent exact load balance because the arrival composition changes over the horizon. We therefore use a conservative domination argument. Since Δ​Tb≤Δ​T[1,…,m]\Delta T_{b}\leq\Delta T_{[1,\dots,m]} (the service-normalized time for a full batch containing all mm types), the arrivals during any realized service period are dominated by arrivals over a full service-normalized window. This gives the process {W¯(1)b}\{\bar{W}_{(1)}^{b}\}:

W¯(1)b+1=W¯(1)b+Y¯(1)b−n1⋅𝟏{W¯(1)b+Y¯(1)b≥n1},Y¯(1)b∼Poisson(∑j=1m𝒜j(ζ)(t(b),ΔT[1,…,m])).\bar{W}_{(1)}^{b+1}=\bar{W}_{(1)}^{b}+\bar{Y}_{(1)}^{b}-n_{1}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{\bar{W}_{(1)}^{b}+\bar{Y}_{(1)}^{b}\geq n_{1}\},\quad\bar{Y}_{(1)}^{b}\sim\text{Poisson}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathcal{A}_{j}^{(\zeta)}(t(b),\Delta T_{[1,\dots,m]})\Big).

By (15), the aggregate arrival count during any full service-normalized window is bounded by the worst-case quantity Λπ<n1\Lambda^{\pi}<n_{1}. This enables a time-invariant dominating process that provides tractable bounds:

W~(1)b+1=W~(1)b+Y~(1)b−n1⋅𝟏{W~(1)b+Y~(1)b≥n1},Y~(1)b∼Poisson(Λπ).\tilde{W}_{(1)}^{b+1}=\tilde{W}_{(1)}^{b}+\tilde{Y}_{(1)}^{b}-n_{1}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{\tilde{W}_{(1)}^{b}+\tilde{Y}_{(1)}^{b}\geq n_{1}\},\quad\tilde{Y}_{(1)}^{b}\sim\text{Poisson}(\Lambda^{\pi}).

This time-invariant process enables the same queueing bound used in the constant-rate proof. Define X(1)b=Y~(1)b−n1X_{(1)}^{b}=\tilde{Y}_{(1)}^{b}-n_{1}. The process {W~(1)b}\{\tilde{W}_{(1)}^{b}\} is dominated by a Lindley process:

W¯(1)0=2​n1,W¯(1)b+1=max⁡{2​n1,W¯(1)b+X(1)b},∀b∈ℕ.\overline{W}_{(1)}^{0}=2n_{1},\quad\overline{W}_{(1)}^{b+1}=\max\{2n_{1},\overline{W}_{(1)}^{b}+X_{(1)}^{b}\},\quad\forall b\in\mathbb{N}.

Thus we have the dominance chain:

W(1)b≤W¯(1)b≤W~(1)b≤W¯(1)b,∀b∈ℕ.W_{(1)}^{b}\leq\bar{W}_{(1)}^{b}\leq\tilde{W}_{(1)}^{b}\leq\overline{W}_{(1)}^{b},\quad\forall b\in\mathbb{N}.

Since n1>Λπn_{1}>\Lambda^{\pi}, the process {W¯(1)b}\{\overline{W}_{(1)}^{b}\} has negative drift. By Kingman’s inequality (Kingman, 1962), with

Var​(X(1)b)=Λπ,|𝔼⁡[X(1)b]|=n1−Λπ,\text{Var}(X_{(1)}^{b})=\Lambda^{\pi},\quad\left|\mathbb{E}\left[X_{(1)}^{b}\right]\right|=n_{1}-\Lambda^{\pi},

we obtain

𝔼⁡[W(1)b]≤2​n1+𝔼⁡[(Y~(1)b−n1)2]2​(n1−Λπ).\mathbb{E}\left[W_{(1)}^{b}\right]\leq 2n_{1}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\tilde{Y}_{(1)}^{b}-n_{1})^{2}]}{2\left(n_{1}-\Lambda^{\pi}\right)}.

F.2 Subsequent Segments Analysis (k≥2k\geq 2)

For segment kk (2≤k≤m2\leq k\leq m), arrivals come from prompts that completed segment k−1k-1. The batch index bb for segment kk counts only batches containing segment k−1k-1. These indices differ across segments but are bounded by the total batch count BB. As in Appendix E, W(k)bW^{b}_{(k)} is the post-review carryover residual at the downstream boundary; fresh survivors from segment k−1k-1 are charged to the upstream threshold batch, and only residual carryover receives the extra safety buffer.

Time-varying thinning probabilities.

Consider the bb-th arrival to segment kk, which comes from the bb-th batch containing segment k−1k-1. The thinning probabilities depend on the prompt arrival times in this batch and vary over time. For a prompt that has reached boundary k−1k-1 at physical time ss, its conditional continuation probability is the instantaneous ratio ∑j=kmλjs/∑j=k−1mλjs\sum_{j=k}^{m}\lambda_{j}^{s}/\sum_{j=k-1}^{m}\lambda_{j}^{s} when the denominator is positive. Because the intensities are continuous and pk∗p_{k}^{*} is the supremum over arbitrarily short positive windows in Section A.1, this instantaneous ratio is at most pk∗p_{k}^{*}. If the prompts in a boundary batch accumulated over a longer interval, the aggregate continuation ratio is a denominator-weighted average of positive-denominator subwindow ratios of length at most Δπ\Delta^{\pi}, and is therefore also bounded by pk∗p_{k}^{*}. Thus, conditional on the filtration before boundary revelation, the survivor indicators in a boundary batch are independent Bernoulli random variables with possibly different probabilities qi≤pk∗q_{i}\leq p_{k}^{*}. Their sum Y(k)bY_{(k)}^{b} is Poisson-binomial and is stochastically dominated by Binomial⁡(nk−1,pk∗)\mathrm{Binomial}(n_{k-1},p_{k}^{*}). Equivalently, using shared uniforms UibU_{i}^{b}, write the actual survivor indicators as 𝟏{Uib≤qi}{\bf 1}\{U_{i}^{b}\leq q_{i}\} and the dominating indicators as 𝟏{Uib≤pk∗}{\bf 1}\{U_{i}^{b}\leq p_{k}^{*}\}; then Y(k)b≤Y¯(k)bY_{(k)}^{b}\leq\bar{Y}_{(k)}^{b} pathwise, where Y¯(k)b∼Binomial⁡(nk−1,pk∗)\bar{Y}_{(k)}^{b}\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n_{k-1},p_{k}^{*}). By (15) and the definition of pk∗p_{k}^{*},

pk∗<nknk−1.p_{k}^{*}<\frac{n_{k}}{n_{k-1}}.

The boundary-arrival count therefore satisfies

Y(k)b≤Y¯(k)b,Y¯(k)b∼Binomial​(nk−1,pk∗),∀b≥0,Y_{(k)}^{b}\leq\bar{Y}_{(k)}^{b},\quad\bar{Y}_{(k)}^{b}\sim\text{Binomial}(n_{k-1},p_{k}^{*}),\quad\forall b\geq 0,

and the state transition rule is

W(k)b+1=W(k)b+Y(k)b−nk⋅𝟏{W(k)b+Y(k)b≥nk},W_{(k)}^{b+1}=W_{(k)}^{b}+Y_{(k)}^{b}-n_{k}\cdot\mathbf{1}\{W_{(k)}^{b}+Y_{(k)}^{b}\geq n_{k}\},

where bb indexes batches containing segment k−1k-1, since new arrivals to segment kk occur only when segment k−1k-1 is processed.

Define X(k)b=Y(k)b−nkX_{(k)}^{b}=Y_{(k)}^{b}-n_{k}. Although Y(k)bY_{(k)}^{b} is Poisson-binomial and time-varying, the coupling construction follows the same induction as Appendix G.4:

Lemma 18 (Coupling for Time-Varying Case).

Define a coupled process {W~(k)b}\{\tilde{W}_{(k)}^{b}\} by:

W~(k)0\displaystyle\tilde{W}_{(k)}^{0} =nk,\displaystyle=n_{k},
W~(k)b+1\displaystyle\tilde{W}_{(k)}^{b+1} =max⁡{nk,W~(k)b+X(k)b},\displaystyle=\max\{n_{k},\,\tilde{W}_{(k)}^{b}+X_{(k)}^{b}\},
X(k)b\displaystyle X_{(k)}^{b} =Y(k)b−nk.\displaystyle=Y_{(k)}^{b}-n_{k}.

Then W~(k)b≥W(k)b\tilde{W}^{b}_{(k)}\geq W^{b}_{(k)} for all b∈ℕb\in\mathbb{N}.

To apply Kingman’s inequality (Kingman, 1962), we construct a time-invariant dominating process using the pathwise dominating counts Y¯(k)b\bar{Y}_{(k)}^{b}:

W¯(k)0\displaystyle\bar{W}_{(k)}^{0} =nk,\displaystyle=n_{k},
W¯(k)b+1\displaystyle\bar{W}_{(k)}^{b+1} =max⁡{nk,W¯(k)b+X¯(k)b},\displaystyle=\max\{n_{k},\,\bar{W}_{(k)}^{b}+\bar{X}_{(k)}^{b}\},
X¯(k)b\displaystyle\bar{X}_{(k)}^{b} =Y¯(k)b−nk,\displaystyle=\bar{Y}_{(k)}^{b}-n_{k},
Y¯(k)b\displaystyle\bar{Y}_{(k)}^{b} ∼Binomial(nk−1,pk∗),∀b∈ℕ.\displaystyle\sim\text{Binomial}(n_{k-1},p_{k}^{*}),\quad\forall b\in\mathbb{N}.

Because the Lindley update is monotone in both the current state and the increment, the shared-uniform coupling gives the dominance chain:

W¯(k)b≥W~(k)b≥W(k)b,∀b∈ℕ.\bar{W}^{b}_{(k)}\geq\tilde{W}^{b}_{(k)}\geq W^{b}_{(k)},\quad\forall b\in\mathbb{N}.

The process W¯(k)b\bar{W}^{b}_{(k)} has the Lindley representation:

W¯(k)0\displaystyle\bar{W}_{(k)}^{0} =nk,\displaystyle=n_{k},
W¯(k)b+1\displaystyle\bar{W}_{(k)}^{b+1} =nk+max0≤i≤b⁡{S¯(k)i},\displaystyle=n_{k}+\max_{0\leq i\leq b}\{\bar{S}_{(k)}^{i}\},
where ​S¯(k)0\displaystyle\text{where }\bar{S}_{(k)}^{0} =0,S¯(k)i=∑r=1iX¯(k)r, 1≤i≤b.\displaystyle=0,\;\bar{S}_{(k)}^{i}=\sum_{r=1}^{i}\bar{X}_{(k)}^{r},\;1\leq i\leq b.

Since

𝔼⁡[X¯(k)b]=nk−1⋅pk∗−nk<0,∀b∈ℕ,\mathbb{E}\left[\bar{X}_{(k)}^{b}\right]=n_{k-1}\cdot p_{k}^{*}-n_{k}<0,\quad\forall b\in\mathbb{N},

the coupled process {W¯(k)b}\{\bar{W}_{(k)}^{b}\} has negative drift. With

Var​(X¯(k)b)=nk−1​pk∗​(1−pk∗),|𝔼⁡[X¯(k)b]|=nk−pk∗​nk−1,\text{Var}(\bar{X}_{(k)}^{b})=n_{k-1}p_{k}^{*}(1-p_{k}^{*}),\quad\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\bar{X}_{(k)}^{b}\right]\right|=n_{k}-p_{k}^{*}n_{k-1},

Kingman’s inequality (Kingman, 1962) yields:

𝔼⁡[max0≤i≤b⁡{S¯(k)i}]≤nk−1​pk∗​(1−pk∗)2​(nk−nk−1​pk∗).\mathbb{E}\left[\max_{0\leq i\leq b}\{\bar{S}_{(k)}^{i}\}\right]\leq\frac{n_{k-1}p_{k}^{*}(1-p_{k}^{*})}{2(n_{k}-n_{k-1}p_{k}^{*})}.

Thus, the expected queue length is bounded:

𝔼⁡[W(k)b]≤𝔼⁡[W~(k)b]≤𝔼⁡[W¯(k)b]≤nk+𝔼⁡[(Y¯(k)b−nk)2]2​(nk−nk−1​pk∗).\mathbb{E}\left[W_{(k)}^{b}\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\tilde{W}_{(k)}^{b}\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\bar{W}_{(k)}^{b}\right]\leq n_{k}+\frac{\mathbb{E}[(\bar{Y}_{(k)}^{b}-n_{k})^{2}]}{2(n_{k}-n_{k-1}p_{k}^{*})}.

F.3 Throughput, Delay, and High-Probability Bounds

The bounded queue estimates above imply that the expected terminal unfinished work is O⁡(1)O(1). This includes the first-segment entry queue, the downstream boundary queues, the bounded segment interiors, and the final partial service opportunity. Dividing this terminal work by the scaled horizon ζ​T\zeta T gives

ThroughputT∗−𝔼⁡[Throughput(ζ,π)]=O⁡((ζ​T)−1).\textbf{Throughput}_{T}^{*}-\mathbb{E}[\textbf{Throughput}^{(\zeta,\pi)}]=O((\zeta T)^{-1}).

This argument does not require a lower bound on the arrival rate. If arrivals fall below the first threshold near the end of the horizon, fewer than n1n_{1} prompts can remain in the external entry queue, which is still a bounded terminal effect.

For service-normalized delay, the queue-integral argument from Appendix E applies to the service periods and downstream boundary queues because their expected lengths are uniformly bounded. The only additional issue in the time-varying setting is waiting for the Segment 1 entry queue to reach its threshold during low-arrival intervals. The first-segment waiting condition gives suptζ​𝔼​[τ1(ζ)​(t)]<∞\sup_{t}\zeta\,\mathbb{E}[\tau_{1}^{(\zeta)}(t)]<\infty, so these idle waiting periods add only O⁡(1)O(1) in service-normalized time. Hence

𝔼⁡[Latency(ζ,π)],𝔼⁡[TTFT(ζ,π)]=O⁡(1)\mathbb{E}[\textbf{Latency}^{(\zeta,\pi)}],\mathbb{E}[\textbf{TTFT}^{(\zeta,\pi)}]=O(1)

whenever the first-segment waiting condition holds.

For high-probability memory bounds, the analysis follows the same martingale construction applied to the time-invariant coupled process {W¯(k)b}\{\bar{W}_{(k)}^{b}\} defined above. Each realized iteration has duration at least d0/ζd_{0}/\zeta, so the number of realized opportunities over [0,T][0,T] is at most Bζmax=⌈ζ​T/d0⌉B_{\zeta}^{\max}=\lceil\zeta T/d_{0}\rceil. By the same argument as in Appendix E, with X¯(k)r=Y¯(k)r−nk\bar{X}_{(k)}^{r}=\bar{Y}_{(k)}^{r}-n_{k}, Y¯(k)r∼Binomial​(nk−1,pk∗)\bar{Y}_{(k)}^{r}\sim\text{Binomial}(n_{k-1},p_{k}^{*}), and pk∗<nk/nk−1<1p_{k}^{*}<n_{k}/n_{k-1}<1, the memory bound is:

Mreq,tv(ζ,π)=Mπ+∑k=2mnk⋅(l+lk−1′)+∑k=2mθk−1​ln⁡(m⁡(1+ζ​T/d0)δ)⋅(l+lk−1′),M_{\mathrm{req},\mathrm{tv}}^{(\zeta,\pi)}=M^{\pi}+\sum_{k=2}^{m}n_{k}\cdot(l+l_{k-1}^{\prime})+\sum_{k=2}^{m}\theta_{k}^{-1}\ln\left(\frac{m(1+\zeta T/d_{0})}{\delta}\right)\cdot(l+l_{k-1}^{\prime}),

where θk\theta_{k} (2≤k≤m2\leq k\leq m) is the unique positive solution to:

e−θk​nk​(1−pk∗+pk∗​eθk)nk−1=1.e^{-\theta_{k}n_{k}}(1-p_{k}^{*}+p_{k}^{*}e^{\theta_{k}})^{n_{k-1}}=1. (20)

Since pk∗p_{k}^{*} is used to dominate every realized thinning probability, the same exponential-martingale argument as Appendix G.5 applies with this worst-case binomial increment. The lower bound for θk\theta_{k} follows from the same calculation.

Let ℰtv\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tv}} be the event that every downstream boundary residual is bounded by the corresponding deterministic-plus-logarithmic buffer in Mreq,tv(ζ,π)M_{\mathrm{req},\mathrm{tv}}^{(\zeta,\pi)} over all opportunities up to BζmaxB_{\zeta}^{\max}. The preceding martingale bound and a union bound over downstream segments give ℙ⁡(ℰtv)≥1−δ\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tv}})\geq 1-\delta. Couple the finite-memory Nested WAIT implementation to the time-varying threshold-controlled comparison dynamics on the same arrivals and continuation marks until the first memory repair. On ℰtv\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tv}}, the same resident-boundary accounting as in Appendix E applies: threshold-controlled interiors are charged to MπM^{\pi}, fresh survivors are charged to the just-processed upstream batch, and only carryover resident boundary residuals require the logarithmic buffers. Hence the projected resident memory is at most Mreq,tv(ζ,π)≤CM_{\mathrm{req},\mathrm{tv}}^{(\zeta,\pi)}\leq C at both repair sites. Therefore memory repair is not invoked on ℰtv\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tv}}, the finite-memory implementation coincides with the comparison dynamics on [0,T][0,T], and no memory-overflow-induced evictions occur on that event.

It remains to transfer the comparison-dynamics estimates to the finite-memory implementation without conditioning on ℰtv\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tv}}. Let ATA_{T} be the total number of external arrivals over [0,T][0,T]. Then ATA_{T} is Poisson with mean

μT=ζ​∫0T∑j=1mλju​𝑑u.\mu_{T}=\zeta\int_{0}^{T}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\lambda_{j}^{u}\,du.

The uniform upper bound on arrival rates gives μT=O⁡(ζ​T)\mu_{T}=O(\zeta T). For any event FF with ℙ⁡(F)≤δ\mathbb{P}(F)\leq\delta, the same Poisson split as in Theorem 7 gives

𝔼⁡[AT​𝟏F]≤2​μT​δ+C1​μT​e−c1​μT\mathbb{E}[A_{T}{\bf 1}_{F}]\leq 2\mu_{T}\delta+C_{1}\mu_{T}e^{-c_{1}\mu_{T}}

for constants C1,c1>0C_{1},c_{1}>0, with no independence requirement between FF and ATA_{T}. Taking F=ℰtvcF=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tv}}^{c}, the bad-event throughput contribution is at most lm′​𝔼​[AT​𝟏ℰtvc]/(ζ​T)=O⁡((ζ​T)−1)l_{m}^{\prime}\mathbb{E}[A_{T}{\bf 1}_{\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tv}}^{c}}]/(\zeta T)=O((\zeta T)^{-1}), because δ≤K​(1+ζ​T)−1\delta\leq K(1+\zeta T)^{-1} and supμ≥0μ​e−c1​μ<∞\sup_{\mu\geq 0}\mu e^{-c_{1}\mu}<\infty.

For delay and TTFT, the theorem invokes the first-segment waiting condition. Under this lower-side condition in the bounded-rate model, μT=Θ⁡(ζ​T)\mu_{T}=\Theta(\zeta T). Hence the finite-horizon censored bad-event contribution, normalized by 𝔼⁡[AT]=μT\mathbb{E}[A_{T}]=\mu_{T}, is at most

ζ​T​𝔼⁡[AT​𝟏ℰtvc]μT≤ζ​T​(2​δ+C1​e−c1​μT)=O⁡(1).\zeta T\frac{\mathbb{E}[A_{T}{\bf 1}_{\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tv}}^{c}}]}{\mu_{T}}\leq\zeta T\left(2\delta+C_{1}e^{-c_{1}\mu_{T}}\right)=O(1).

Combining these bad-event bounds with the comparison-dynamics estimates above gives the stated unconditional finite-memory performance bounds and the eviction probability bound.

Appendix G Proof of Lemmas

Throughout this section, we use bb for the embedded review index and BB for the total number of review slots.

G.1 Proof of Lemma 10

Write nn for the critical single-type threshold, so Xb∼Poisson⁡(n)X^{b}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(n). Taking expectations on both sides of the state transition equation gives

𝔼⁡[Wb+1]=𝔼⁡[Wb]+n−n​ℙ​(Wb+Xb≥n).\mathbb{E}\left[W^{b+1}\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[W^{b}\right]+n-n\mathbb{P}(W^{b}+X^{b}\geq n).

Summing from b=0b=0 to B−1B-1, and noting that W0=0W^{0}=0, we obtain

𝔼⁡[WB]=n​B−n​𝔼​[B−Bstuck]=n⋅𝔼⁡[Bstuck].\mathbb{E}\left[W^{B}\right]=nB-n\mathbb{E}\left[B-B_{\text{stuck}}\right]=n\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[B_{\text{stuck}}\right].

G.2 Proof of Lemma 11

We prove by induction on the review index bb. The coupled process {W~b}\{\tilde{W}^{b}\} starts with a safety buffer of 2​n2n, compared to the embedded review process starting at 0, ensuring it remains above Wb+nW^{b}+n throughout. For the inductive step, we consider two cases based on whether the review process removes a threshold batch or experiences a stuck review slot.

Base case.

For b=0b=0, W~0=2​n≥n=W0+n\tilde{W}^{0}=2n\geq n=W^{0}+n.

Inductive step.

Assume W~b≥Wb+n\tilde{W}^{b}\geq W^{b}+n for some b≥0b\geq 0. We show W~b+1≥Wb+1+n\tilde{W}^{b+1}\geq W^{b+1}+n by considering two cases:

Case 1 (Threshold batch removed): If Wb+Xb≥nW^{b}+X^{b}\geq n, the queue has accumulated enough prompts to remove a threshold batch, so Wb+1=Wb+Xb−nW^{b+1}=W^{b}+X^{b}-n. Then

W~b+1=max⁡{2​n,W~b+Xb−n}≥W~b+Xb−n≥(Wb+n)+Xb−n=Wb+1+n.\tilde{W}^{b+1}=\max\{2n,\tilde{W}^{b}+X^{b}-n\}\geq\tilde{W}^{b}+X^{b}-n\geq(W^{b}+n)+X^{b}-n=W^{b+1}+n.

Case 2 (Stuck review slot): If Wb+Xb<nW^{b}+X^{b}<n, insufficient prompts are available and the review process cannot remove a threshold batch. The queue simply accumulates arrivals: Wb+1=Wb+XbW^{b+1}=W^{b}+X^{b}. The safety buffer ensures dominance:

W~b+1=max⁡{2​n,W~b+Xb−n}≥2​n>Wb+1+n.\tilde{W}^{b+1}=\max\{2n,\tilde{W}^{b}+X^{b}-n\}\geq 2n>W^{b+1}+n.

By induction, W~b≥Wb+n\tilde{W}^{b}\geq W^{b}+n for all b∈ℕb\in\mathbb{N}.

G.3 Proof of Lemma 17

The lemma compares the type-jj entry queue in the periodic comparison system with a reflected random walk that always subtracts njn_{j} after adding one slot of arrivals, but never falls below the safety level 2​nj2n_{j}. Fix type jj and write W¯b=W¯(j)b\bar{W}^{b}=\bar{W}^{b}_{(j)}, W~b=W~(j)b\widetilde{W}^{b}=\widetilde{W}^{b}_{(j)}, n=njn=n_{j}, and X¯b=X¯(j)b\bar{X}^{b}=\bar{X}^{b}_{(j)}. We prove by induction that W~b≥W¯b\widetilde{W}^{b}\geq\bar{W}^{b}.

The claim holds at b=0b=0, since W~0=2​n\widetilde{W}^{0}=2n and W¯0=0\bar{W}^{0}=0. Suppose W~b≥W¯b\widetilde{W}^{b}\geq\bar{W}^{b}. If W¯b+X¯b≥n\bar{W}^{b}+\bar{X}^{b}\geq n, then the comparison queue serves nn prompts and

W¯b+1=W¯b+X¯b−n.\bar{W}^{b+1}=\bar{W}^{b}+\bar{X}^{b}-n.

Using the induction hypothesis,

W~b+1=max⁡{2​n,W~b+X¯b−n}≥W~b+X¯b−n≥W¯b+1.\widetilde{W}^{b+1}=\max\{2n,\widetilde{W}^{b}+\bar{X}^{b}-n\}\geq\widetilde{W}^{b}+\bar{X}^{b}-n\geq\bar{W}^{b+1}.

If W¯b+X¯b<n\bar{W}^{b}+\bar{X}^{b}<n, then no type-jj service occurs in the comparison queue and W¯b+1=W¯b+X¯b<n\bar{W}^{b+1}=\bar{W}^{b}+\bar{X}^{b}<n. In this case W~b+1≥2​n>W¯b+1\widetilde{W}^{b+1}\geq 2n>\bar{W}^{b+1}. Thus the domination holds for all bb, and the argument applies independently to every type jj.

G.4 Nested WAIT Coupling Bound

This lemma is used when a downstream boundary queue receives binomially thinned arrivals from the previous segment. We index the queue after the threshold review at the start of an opportunity in which the previous segment is processed. If the downstream boundary already has a threshold batch, Nested WAIT removes that batch in the same prefix batch; newly surviving prompts generated by the previous segment are treated as fresh boundary input for the next review.

Let W(k)bW^{b}_{(k)} be the residual resident boundary queue for segment k≥2k\geq 2 after this review, and let Y(k)bY^{b}_{(k)} be the number of newly surviving prompts at the next boundary-crossing opportunity. The queue satisfies

W(k)b+1≤W(k)b+Y(k)b−nk𝟏{W(k)b+Y(k)b≥nk}.W^{b+1}_{(k)}\leq W^{b}_{(k)}+Y^{b}_{(k)}-n_{k}{\bf 1}\{W^{b}_{(k)}+Y^{b}_{(k)}\geq n_{k}\}.

Define X(k)b=Y(k)b−nkX^{b}_{(k)}=Y^{b}_{(k)}-n_{k} and

W~(k)0=nk,W~(k)b+1=max⁡{nk,W~(k)b+X(k)b}.\tilde{W}_{(k)}^{0}=n_{k},\qquad\tilde{W}_{(k)}^{b+1}=\max\{n_{k},\tilde{W}_{(k)}^{b}+X^{b}_{(k)}\}.

We prove by induction that W~(k)b≥W(k)b\tilde{W}^{b}_{(k)}\geq W^{b}_{(k)}. At b=0b=0, the domination holds because W~(k)0=nk\tilde{W}^{0}_{(k)}=n_{k} and W(k)0=0W^{0}_{(k)}=0. Suppose it holds at bb. If W(k)b≥nkW^{b}_{(k)}\geq n_{k}, then

W(k)b+1≤W(k)b+Y(k)b−nk≤W~(k)b+X(k)b≤W~(k)b+1.W^{b+1}_{(k)}\leq W^{b}_{(k)}+Y^{b}_{(k)}-n_{k}\leq\tilde{W}^{b}_{(k)}+X^{b}_{(k)}\leq\tilde{W}^{b+1}_{(k)}.

If W(k)b<nkW^{b}_{(k)}<n_{k} but W(k)b+Y(k)b≥nkW^{b}_{(k)}+Y^{b}_{(k)}\geq n_{k}, a threshold batch is removed at the next boundary review, and

W(k)b+1≤W(k)b+Y(k)b−nk≤W~(k)b+X(k)b≤W~(k)b+1.W^{b+1}_{(k)}\leq W^{b}_{(k)}+Y^{b}_{(k)}-n_{k}\leq\tilde{W}^{b}_{(k)}+X^{b}_{(k)}\leq\tilde{W}^{b+1}_{(k)}.

If W(k)b+Y(k)b<nkW^{b}_{(k)}+Y^{b}_{(k)}<n_{k}, then

W(k)b+1=W(k)b+Y(k)b<nk≤W~(k)b+1.W^{b+1}_{(k)}=W^{b}_{(k)}+Y^{b}_{(k)}<n_{k}\leq\tilde{W}^{b+1}_{(k)}.

Thus the domination holds for all b∈ℕb\in\mathbb{N}.

G.5 Martingale Root Bound for Nested WAIT

This auxiliary calculation records the exponential tilting parameter used in the high-probability memory bound. Let 0<pk<nk/nk−1<10<p_{k}<n_{k}/n_{k-1}<1, let Y¯∼Binomial⁡(nk−1,pk)\bar{Y}\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n_{k-1},p_{k}), and set X=Y¯−nkX=\bar{Y}-n_{k}. The moment-generating equation

𝔼⁡[eθ​X]=e−θ​nk​(1−pk+pk​eθ)nk−1=1\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta X}]=e^{-\theta n_{k}}(1-p_{k}+p_{k}e^{\theta})^{n_{k-1}}=1

has a unique positive solution θk\theta_{k}. This is the standard Cramer–Lundberg root for a negative-drift random walk with bounded positive jumps (Asmussen, 2003, see, e.g.,). With S(k)i=∑r=1iX(k)rS^{i}_{(k)}=\sum_{r=1}^{i}X^{r}_{(k)}, the process eθk​S(k)ie^{\theta_{k}S^{i}_{(k)}} is therefore a mean-one martingale, and Doob’s maximal inequality (Durrett, 2019, see, e.g.,) yields

ℙ⁡(max0≤i≤r⁡S(k)i≥x)≤e−θk​x.\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{0\leq i\leq r}S^{i}_{(k)}\geq x\right)\leq e^{-\theta_{k}x}.

We will use the corresponding finite-horizon bound for the reflected process

Z(k)0=0,Z(k)b+1=max⁡{0,Z(k)b+X(k)b}.Z^{0}_{(k)}=0,\qquad Z^{b+1}_{(k)}=\max\{0,Z^{b}_{(k)}+X^{b}_{(k)}\}.

If max0≤b≤B⁡Z(k)b≥x\max_{0\leq b\leq B}Z^{b}_{(k)}\geq x, then some excursion of the random walk has gained at least xx: there are 0≤a<b≤B0\leq a<b\leq B such that ∑r=ab−1X(k)r≥x\sum_{r=a}^{b-1}X^{r}_{(k)}\geq x. Applying the preceding maximal inequality from each possible excursion start and unioning over at most BB starts gives

ℙ⁡(max0≤b≤B⁡Z(k)b≥x)≤B​e−θk​x,B≥1.\mathbb{P}\left(\max_{0\leq b\leq B}Z^{b}_{(k)}\geq x\right)\leq Be^{-\theta_{k}x},\qquad B\geq 1.

For completeness, we also record the elementary drift-to-root bound used in the theorem. Writing D=nk−nk−1​pk>0D=n_{k}-n_{k-1}p_{k}>0 and g⁡(θ)=log⁡𝔼⁡[eθ​X]g(\theta)=\log\mathbb{E}[e^{\theta X}], we have g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0, g′​(0)=−Dg^{\prime}(0)=-D, and g′′​(θ)≤nk−1/4g^{\prime\prime}(\theta)\leq n_{k-1}/4. Applying Taylor’s theorem at the positive root g⁡(θk)=0g(\theta_{k})=0 gives

θk≥8​(nk−nk−1​pk)nk−1.\displaystyle\theta_{k}\geq\frac{8(n_{k}-n_{k-1}p_{k})}{n_{k-1}}. (21)

Appendix H Additional Experiments

This appendix reports supplemental robustness and implementation-fidelity analyses for Section 6. Section H.1 records the full event-driven Nested WAIT pseudocode used for implementation. Section H.2 isolates the role of the accumulation requirement by comparing WAIT with a threshold-only variant. Section H.3 validates the simulator against direct GPU measurements and reports supplemental physical-GPU comparisons on single-type and real-data workloads. Section H.4 examines repeated-run variability near the observed transition from near-overloaded to overloaded operation, and Section H.5 evaluates the policy in a prefill-decode-disaggregated deployment.

H.1 Nested WAIT implementation pseudocode

Algorithm H.1 gives the event-driven implementation corresponding to the main-text description in Algorithm 2. It makes explicit the queue transitions at segment boundaries and the resident-boundary memory-repair rule.

H.2 Threshold without waiting

We isolate the role of waiting on the single-type p512d20 workload by comparing full WAIT with a threshold-only variant, denoted WAIT-no-wait. For each arrival rate, the two policies use the same parameter setting and hence the same threshold upper bound. The threshold-only variant enforces this upper bound but does not wait for enough requests to accumulate before service. The comparison therefore holds the admission-capacity scale fixed and changes only whether service is delayed to form a full threshold batch.

Figure 16 reports the comparison across arrival rates. At low arrival rates, waiting introduces a modest latency cost: requests may wait to accumulate even when the server has enough capacity to process them immediately. This cost shrinks as the arrival rate increases. Near the overload boundary, waiting becomes useful because it regulates the timing at which work enters service, reducing latency relative to the threshold-only variant. Once the system is overloaded, the upper bound becomes the dominant control, and the two variants again behave similarly.

H.3 Real-GPU validation

We complement the Vidur experiments in Section 6 with measurements on a physical NVIDIA A100 80 GB serving Llama-2-7B. These runs serve two purposes. First, direct GPU measurements calibrate the iteration-time model used by Vidur. Second, we implement WAIT’s admission logic using SGLang 0.5.7, an open-source LLM serving framework (SGLang Team, 2024), and test the resulting scheduler in end-to-end GPU runs. We report three comparisons: iteration-time measurements against Vidur’s prediction, a single-type GPU workload corresponding to Section 6.1, and a real-data GPU workload corresponding to Section 6.2.

Simulator vs GPU.

To calibrate the simulator in the operating region used in Section 6, we compare Vidur’s iteration-time predictions with direct measurements on the same A100 80 GB GPU running Llama-2-7B under the SGLang baseline scheduler. Vidur’s raw Llama-2-7B attention profiling covers batch sizes up to 128128. Within this profiled range, the validation uses batch sizes B∈{1,2,4,…,128}B\in\{1,2,4,\ldots,128\} with prefill length 256256 and decode length 2020; we also test extrapolation to B=256B=256. In Figure 17, each point is one batch-size configuration: the horizontal coordinate is the measured GPU batch inference time, and the vertical coordinate is Vidur’s prediction. Points near the y=xy=x line therefore indicate accurate simulator predictions. On the plotted grid, the fitted linear iteration-time model has mean absolute percentage error 1.93%1.93\% and R2=0.9943R^{2}=0.9943; extrapolation to B=256B=256 has absolute percentage error 4.93%4.93\%. The fitted intercept and slope are d0≈276d_{0}\approx 276 ms and d1≈0.0115d_{1}\approx 0.0115 ms per KV-cache token, respectively, consistent with the time model in Equation (1). This agreement supports the Vidur-based latency and operating-range comparisons in Section 6 for the workloads studied here.

Single-type workload on GPU.

Using the same single-type workload as Section 6.1, we run end-to-end SGLang experiments with Poisson arrivals at λ∈{1,2,…,15}\lambda\in\{1,2,\ldots,15\} requests/s and 500500 prompts per rate. The SGLang baseline scheduler uses chunked_prefill_size=256=256 and prefill_max_requests=8=8; its default configuration triggers memory-overflow failures at several mid-to-high rates and is therefore not a feasible baseline on this workload. WAIT uses the same parameter values at all rates. Its system-wide batch-size cap is tl=21\mathrm{tl}=21, and its per-stage WAIT threshold is n1=1n_{1}=1. The chunk size is 384384, so a prefill of length 512512 is processed as K=⌈512/384⌉=2K=\lceil 512/384\rceil=2 prefill blocks before the request enters the 2020 decode-token stages. Thus, the single-type pipeline has K+20=22K+20=22 stages: WAIT schedules at most one request from each active stage, while tl=21\mathrm{tl}=21 caps how many requests can be served concurrently across these stages. The SGLang patch implements this policy through the batch-size cap and the per-request prefill chunk cap; a transition block of size 1010 switches the scheduler back to SGLang’s native rule in lightly loaded states. Figure 18 reports mean end-to-end latency as λ\lambda varies. Under this GPU configuration, WAIT is consistently lower-latency than the feasible SGLang baseline scheduler, with an average reduction of 29.7%29.7\% across the arrival-rate grid.

Real dataset on GPU.

Using the same lmsys-chat-1m workload distribution as Section 6.2, we run paired SGLang experiments with Poisson arrivals at λ∈{0.1,0.2,…,0.7}\lambda\in\{0.1,0.2,\ldots,0.7\} requests/s and 200200 prompts per rate. The server is restarted before each rate so that the SGLang baseline and Nested WAIT are compared from the same clean GPU state. Nested WAIT uses chunk size 384384 and a rate-specific system-wide batch-size cap tl\mathrm{tl}. For the real-data runs, tl\mathrm{tl} is distributed over the decode horizon through the listed segment partitions, using the same continuation-based allocation described in Section 6.2. Table 4 reports the batch-size caps and decode-stage partitions used in these GPU runs. Figure 19 reports mean end-to-end latency in absolute units. Across the tested rates, Nested WAIT has lower latency than the SGLang baseline, with the largest reduction at λ=0.6\lambda=0.6 and an average reduction of 3.6%3.6\%.

H.4 Repeated-run variability

The main arrival-rate figures in Section 6 report averages over 1010 independent simulation replications at each plotted configuration. To examine sampling variability near the observed transition from near-overloaded to overloaded operation, we additionally repeat the near-transition configurations 2020 times and report the corresponding deviations.

The repeated-run diagnostic preserves the same latency ordering as the main figures across independent arrival draws.

H.5 Prefill-decode-disaggregated deployment

Production LLM serving increasingly uses a prefill-decode disaggregation (PD) architecture, in which prefill and decode are executed by separate services and the KV cache is transferred between them (Patel et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024). This architecture aligns more closely with the memory-dependent timing model in Section 2. Because the decode server no longer mixes prefill and decode work, each iteration processes one token for each active post-prefill job, and the iteration time is driven primarily by active KV-cache usage. The linear iteration-time model in (1) is therefore especially appropriate in this setting. The corresponding control decision is how many post-prefill jobs to keep in concurrent decoding; the WAIT threshold implements this decision as an upper bound on the decode-side service population.

We implement this setting in Vidur by using a decode-only request generator: each request enters the simulated decode server after prefill has completed, with post-prefill context length 630630 tokens and decode length 2020 (p630d20). Arrivals follow a Poisson process with λ∈{100,150,…,500}\lambda\in\{100,150,\ldots,500\} requests/s. In this decode-only setting, Sarathi’s chunked-prefill rule no longer changes the scheduling decision, so vLLM’s PD scheduler (vLLM (PD)) represents the baseline. Figure 20 reports mean end-to-end decode latency: WAIT improves over vLLM at every rate, with the relative gap ranging from 45%45\% at λ=100\lambda=100 to 55%55\% at λ=500\lambda=500. Thus, in this tested decode-only setting, the threshold rule improves delay by controlling the decode-side batch composition.
